94617.m: Thin sections show where the clay of ancient pottery came from.

94618.q: With crossed polarisers, how are the polariser and the analyser positioned relative to each other?
94618.e: The analyser then only lets through light whose direction of vibration has been changed in the mineral. Without a sample the image stays black.
94618.m: With crossed polarisers the empty field of view is dark.

94619.q: What do geologists use a polarising microscope for?
a: To identify minerals in wafer-thin slices of rock
To measure the age of fossils
To observe stars in the night sky
94619.e: Minerals change polarised light in typical ways. This makes it possible to recognise the components of a rock.
94619.m: A polarising microscope is used to identify minerals in rock.

94620.q: Which property of anisotropic minerals causes the interference colours in a polarising microscope?
94620.e: In the crystal, light is split into two rays travelling at different speeds. After the analyser, the path difference leads to interference and therefore to colours.
94620.m: Birefringence produces the bright colours in a polarising microscope.

94621.q: Why is rock ground into a very thin slice (thin section) for the polarising microscope?
a: So that light shines through the minerals
So that the rock becomes lighter
So that the rock is no longer radioactive
So that it fits on a postage stamp
94621.e: A thin section is only about 0.03 millimetres thick. This makes most minerals transparent so they can be examined in transmitted light.
94621.m: A thin section is so thin that light shines through it.

a: Light that vibrates in only one direction
Light that comes from the North Pole
94622.e: Ordinary light vibrates in all directions at right angles to its direction of travel. A polarising filter lets through only one direction of vibration.
94622.m: Polarised light vibrates in only one direction.

94623.q: A mineral such as biotite changes colour in polarised light when it is rotated. Why is that?
a: It absorbs light to different degrees depending on the direction of vibration
It reflects the colour of the lamp
94623.e: Coloured crystals absorb light to different degrees depending on direction. This is called pleochroism; biotite, for example, changes between light and dark brown.
94623.m: Some minerals change colour in polarised light.

94624.q: Through which clear mineral do you see writing double because it refracts light doubly to a very strong degree?
94624.e: Clear calcite, also called Iceland spar, splits a ray of light into two rays. That is why everything you look at through it appears double.
94624.m: Calcite refracts light so strongly in two that you see images double.

94625.q: To which mineral group, the most common in the Earth's crust, does plagioclase belong?
94625.e: Feldspars make up about half of the Earth's crust. Plagioclase and alkali feldspar are their two main groups.
94625.m: Plagioclase is a feldspar, the most common mineral group in the crust.

94626.q: Which minerals always stay black in the transmitted light of a polarising microscope?
a: Opaque ore minerals such as pyrite
94626.e: Ore minerals let no light through, even in a thin section. They are therefore examined with a reflected light microscope that lights up the surface.
94626.m: Ore minerals are opaque in transmitted light.

94627.q: How do hydrothermal ore deposits form?
a: Hot watery solutions deposit metals in cracks
Living things collect metals in their bones
94627.e: Deep underground, hot water dissolves metals and carries them through fissures. When it cools or reacts chemically, ore minerals are deposited and form veins.
94627.m: Hydrothermal solutions carry metals into cracks in the rock.

94628.q: What is deposited at black smokers on the seabed?
a: Metal-bearing minerals such as copper and zinc sulphides
94628.e: At mid-ocean ridges, hot water rich in metals pours out and cools suddenly in the seawater. Sulphides of copper, zinc and iron are deposited.
94628.m: Black smokers deposit metal sulphides on the seabed.

94629.q: What do the ancient banded iron formations, which are important sources of iron today, show?
a: That iron dissolved in the early ocean was precipitated by oxygen
That there used to be iron volcanoes
That people were already smelting iron billions of years ago
That meteorites brought all the iron
94629.e: Most banded iron formations are over 2.4 billion years old. Iron dissolved in seawater was oxidised and was deposited in layers of iron oxides and silica.
94629.m: Banded iron formations are billion-year-old deposits of the early oceans.

94630.q: Why can you find gold in the sand of the streams in the Napf area?
a: The heavy gold stays behind where the current slows down
Gold grows back in the stream bed
The gold was lost by the Romans
94630.e: Gold is very heavy and does not weather. Flowing water carries light grains further, and the gold collects in calm places. Such deposits are called placers.
94630.m: In placers, flowing water concentrates heavy minerals.

94631.q: Chile is the world's largest producer of which metal?
94631.e: Chile mines about a quarter of the world's copper. The ores formed above bodies of magma at the subduction zone of the Andes.
94631.m: Chile is the most important copper country in the world.

94632.q: How does bauxite, the most important ore of aluminium, form?
a: Through intense weathering in a tropical climate
94632.e: Heavy rain and warmth wash almost everything out of the rock except aluminium and iron oxides. What remains is a soil rich in aluminium.
94632.m: Bauxite is what is left behind by tropical weathering.

94633.q: In the study of mineral deposits, what is meant by an ore?
a: A mixture of minerals from which metal can be extracted profitably
A mineral with a metallic lustre
A rock from deep in the Earth's mantle
94633.e: What matters is not only the metal content but also whether mining it pays off. If metal prices rise, a deposit that was previously worthless can become an ore.
94633.m: Whether a rock is an ore also depends on the price of the metal.

94634.q: Which mineral is an important iron ore?
94634.e: Haematite (Fe₂O₃) contains about 70 per cent iron. Galena is a lead ore, sphalerite a zinc ore and cassiterite a tin ore.
94634.m: Haematite is one of the most important iron ores.

94635.q: Which symbol is used for amount of substance?
94635.e: Amount of substance is written as n; m stands for mass, N for the number of particles and c for concentration.
94635.m: Amount of substance has the symbol n.

94636.q: In the International System of Units (SI), what kind of quantity is amount of substance?
a: An auxiliary quantity without a unit
94636.e: Amount of substance is one of the seven SI base quantities, alongside length, mass, time, electric current, temperature and luminous intensity.
94636.m: Amount of substance is one of the seven SI base quantities.

94637.q: Which relationship gives the amount of substance n from the mass m and the molar mass M?
94637.e: The molar mass tells you how many grams one mole weighs; dividing the mass by this value gives the number of moles.
94637.m: You get the amount of substance by dividing the mass by the molar mass.

94638.q: What amount of substance is 36 g of water (M about 18 g/mol)?
94638.e: n = m / M = 36 g / 18 g/mol = 2 mol.
94638.m: Twice the mass of the same substance means twice as many moles.

94639.q: What amount of oxygen atoms does 1 mol of sulphuric acid H₂SO₄ contain?
94639.e: Each H₂SO₄ molecule contains 4 oxygen atoms, so 1 mol of sulphuric acid contains 4 mol of oxygen atoms.
94639.m: The subscript in the formula tells you how many moles of an atom are in one mole of the compound.

94640.q: What is the relationship between the number of particles N, the amount of substance n and the Avogadro constant N_A?
94640.e: One mole contains N_A particles, so n moles contain n times as many.
94640.m: The number of particles is the amount of substance multiplied by the Avogadro constant.

94641.q: What amount of ions is produced when 1 mol of aluminium sulphate Al₂(SO₄)₃ dissociates completely in water?
94641.e: Al₂(SO₄)₃ splits into 2 Al³⁺ and 3 SO₄²⁻, so into 5 mol of ions in total.
94641.m: When a salt dissolves, every single ion counts towards the amount of ions.

94642.q: 1 mol of hydrogen gas H₂ and 1 mol of lead are compared. Which quantity is the same for both?
94642.e: One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, about 6.022·10²³; mass, volume and density, on the other hand, depend on the substance.
94642.m: One mole means the same number of particles for every substance.

94643.q: Why do chemists calculate with amounts of substance rather than just masses?
a: Particles react in fixed number ratios
Scales are too inaccurate for this
Amounts of substance do not depend on the substance
94643.e: The coefficients of a chemical equation give ratios of particles and therefore of amounts of substance, not of masses, because different particles have different masses.
94643.m: Chemical equations describe ratios of amounts of substance, not ratios of masses.

94644.q: How has the mole been defined since the 2019 reform of the system of units?
a: By an exactly fixed value of the Avogadro constant
By the mass of the original kilogram in Paris
By the volume of hydrogen at 0 °C
By the charge of an electron
94644.e: Since 20 May 2019 the numerical value of the Avogadro constant has been fixed; so one mole contains an exactly defined number of particles.
94644.m: Since 2019, the mole has been defined by a fixed number of particles.

94645.q: From 1971 to 2019, which portion of substance was the mole defined by?
94645.e: One mole contained as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of the isotope carbon-12; this made the mole depend on the kilogram.
94645.m: The mole used to be tied to the mass of carbon-12.

94646.q: How many base units does the International System of Units SI have, including the mole?
94646.e: The seven base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. The mole was the last to be added, in 1971.
94646.m: The mole is one of the seven SI base units.

94647.q: Which chemist coined the term “mole” (German “Mol”) in 1893?
94647.e: The physical chemist Wilhelm Ostwald, Nobel Prize winner in 1909, introduced the term in his textbook.
94647.m: Wilhelm Ostwald gave the mole its name.

94648.q: From which Latin word is the term “mole” probably derived?
94648.e: Latin “moles” means mass or load; words such as “molecule” (small mass) also come from it.
94648.m: The word mole recalls the Latin moles, meaning mass.

94649.e: 1 mol equals 1,000 mmol, so 0.25 · 1,000 mmol = 250 mmol.
94649.m: One mole equals a thousand millimoles.

94650.q: When do chemistry fans in many countries celebrate “Mole Day”?
94650.e: The date 10/23 in American notation refers to the power of ten in the Avogadro constant.
94650.m: Mole Day on 23 October recalls the size of a mole.

94651.q: Roughly how many atoms does 1 mol of nitrogen molecules N₂ contain?
94651.e: 1 mol of N₂ contains about 6.02·10²³ molecules with 2 atoms each, so about 1.2·10²⁴ atoms.
94651.m: With diatomic molecules, the number of atoms is twice the number of molecules.

94652.q: Roughly how many particles does one mole contain?
94652.e: Since 2019 the Avogadro constant has been fixed at exactly 6.02214076·10²³ per mole. For calculations, 6.022·10²³ is usually enough.
94652.m: One mole contains about 6 times ten to the power of twenty-three particles.

94653.q: What did Amedeo Avogadro suggest in 1811?
a: Equal volumes of gas at the same p and T contain the same number of particles
At the same temperature, the volume of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure
Elements combine in mass ratios of small whole numbers
All gases have the same density at the same temperature
94653.e: Avogadro realised that equal volumes of different (ideal) gases at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of particles.
94653.m: According to Avogadro, the number of particles in a gas depends on volume, pressure and temperature, not on the type of gas.

94654.q: What does the Avogadro constant tell you?
a: The number of particles in one mole
The volume of one mole of gas
The charge of one mole of electrons
94654.e: The Avogadro constant links the amount of substance with the number of particles. One mole of a substance always contains about 6.022·10²³ particles.
94654.m: The Avogadro constant counts the particles in one mole.

94655.q: Roughly what volume does one mole of an ideal gas take up at 0 °C and standard pressure?
94655.e: According to Avogadro, equal volumes of gas contain the same number of particles. That is why one mole of any ideal gas at 0 °C and 1013 hPa takes up about 22.4 litres.
94655.m: One mole of gas has a volume of about 22.4 litres at standard conditions.

94656.q: Which constant do you get if you divide the universal gas constant R by the Avogadro constant?
94656.e: k = R / N_A = 8.314 J/(mol·K) / 6.022·10²³ mol⁻¹ ≈ 1.381·10⁻²³ J/K; it is the gas constant per particle.
94656.m: The Boltzmann constant is the gas constant for a single particle.

94657.q: The Faraday constant is the product of which two values?
a: Elementary charge times the speed of light
94657.e: The Faraday constant is the charge of one mole of elementary charges: F = N_A · e.
94657.m: The Faraday constant is the charge of one mole of electrons.

94658.q: What unit does the Avogadro constant have?
a: none, it is a pure number
94658.e: The Avogadro constant gives the number of particles per mole and so has the unit mol⁻¹; the pure number without a unit is called Avogadro's number.
94658.m: The Avogadro constant has the unit per mole.

94659.q: Roughly how many molecules does 9 g of water (M about 18 g/mol) contain?
94659.e: 9 g of water is 0.5 mol; 0.5 mol · 6.022·10²³ mol⁻¹ ≈ 3.0·10²³ molecules.
94659.m: Half a mole contains half as many particles as a whole mole.

94660.q: Roughly how many atoms does 12 g of carbon-12 contain?
94660.e: 12 g of carbon-12 is exactly one mole. One mole contains about 6.022·10²³ particles.
94660.m: The molar mass in grams always contains about 6 times ten to the power of twenty-three particles.

94661.q: In which unit is molar mass usually given?
94661.e: Molar mass is mass per amount of substance, so grams per mole.
94661.m: Molar mass tells you how many grams one mole of a substance weighs.

94662.q: Roughly what is the molar mass of sulphuric acid H₂SO₄?
94662.m: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of all the atoms in the formula.

94663.q: Roughly what is the molar mass of glucose C₆H₁₂O₆?
94663.m: Glucose has a molar mass of about 180 grams per mole.

94664.q: Roughly what is the molar mass of calcium carbonate CaCO₃?
94664.m: Limestone has a molar mass of about 100 grams per mole.

94665.q: Why is the molar mass of chlorine about 35.45 g/mol and not a whole number?
a: Natural chlorine is a mixture of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37
Chlorine nuclei contain different numbers of protons
Electrons make up almost half of the atomic mass
94665.e: Natural chlorine consists of about three quarters chlorine-35 and one quarter chlorine-37; the average is 35.45.
94665.m: The atomic mass of an element is an average over its natural isotopes.

94666.q: How are the molar mass in g/mol and the molecular mass in u related numerically?
a: The numbers are practically the same
The molar mass is 1,000 times larger
The molar mass is 1,000 times smaller
94666.e: A water molecule weighs about 18 u, a mole of water about 18 g; since 2019 the numbers no longer match exactly, but they agree to many decimal places.
94666.m: The mass of a particle in u and the molar mass in g/mol have almost the same number.

94667.q: Roughly how much does a single water molecule (M about 18 g/mol) weigh?
94667.m: You get the mass of a single particle by dividing the molar mass by the Avogadro constant.

94668.q: One litre of a gas weighs 1.25 g at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa. What is its molar mass (Vm about 22.4 L/mol)?
94668.e: M = density · Vm = 1.25 g/L · 22.4 L/mol = 28 g/mol; that fits nitrogen N₂, for example.
94668.m: The molar mass can be worked out from the density of a gas and the molar volume.

94669.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of sodium hydroxide NaOH (M about 40 g/mol)?
94669.e: m = n · M = 0.25 mol · 40 g/mol = 10 g.
94669.m: Mass is amount of substance multiplied by molar mass.

94670.q: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa?
94670.e: Vm = R · T / p = 8.314 · 273.15 / 101325 m³/mol ≈ 0.0224 m³/mol, so about 22.4 L/mol.
94670.m: At 0 °C and standard pressure, one mole of gas takes up about 22.4 litres.

94671.q: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at 25 °C and 100 kPa?
94671.e: Vm = 8.314 J/(mol·K) · 298.15 K / 100000 Pa ≈ 0.0248 m³/mol, so about 24.8 L/mol.
94671.m: At room temperature the molar volume is larger than at 0 °C.

94672.q: What volume do 3 mol of an ideal gas take up at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa?
94672.e: V = n · Vm = 3 mol · 22.4 L/mol = 67.2 L.
94672.m: The volume of a gas grows in proportion to the amount of substance.

94673.q: What is the mass of 11.2 L of carbon dioxide at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa (M about 44 g/mol)?
94673.m: Using the molar volume, a gas volume can be converted into a mass.

94674.q: Why is the molar volume of liquid water (about 18 mL/mol) so much smaller than that of water vapour?
a: In a gas the distances are much larger than the particles
Water molecules shrink when they condense
Liquid water has a greater molar mass
Water vapour always contains extra air
94674.e: In gases, the space between the particles is huge compared with their own volume; in liquids the particles almost touch.
94674.m: Gases consist mostly of empty space between the particles.

94675.q: What volume does 1 mol of an ideal gas take up at 0 °C if the pressure is 202.65 kPa?
94675.e: The pressure is twice standard pressure, so the volume halves from 22.4 L to 11.2 L.
94675.m: At double the pressure, the molar volume of an ideal gas halves.

94676.q: How much oxygen (at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa) is needed to burn 1 mol of methane completely?
94676.e: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O; 1 mol of methane needs 2 mol of oxygen, so 2 · 22.4 L = 44.8 L.
94676.m: Gas volumes behave like the coefficients in the chemical equation.

94677.q: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at 0 °C if 100 kPa is used as standard pressure?
94677.e: Vm = 8.314 · 273.15 / 100000 m³/mol ≈ 0.0227 m³/mol; the slightly lower pressure makes the volume a little larger.
94677.m: Even small differences in standard pressure change the molar volume.

94678.q: What is the general equation of state for ideal gases?
94678.e: Pressure times volume is proportional to the amount of substance and to the absolute temperature; R is the universal gas constant.
94678.m: For ideal gases, pressure times volume is proportional to amount of substance and absolute temperature.

94679.q: Roughly what is the value of the universal gas constant R?
94679.e: R ≈ 8.314 J/(mol·K) links pressure, volume, amount of substance and temperature in the gas equation.
94679.m: The gas constant is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin.

94680.q: Which assumptions apply in the ideal gas model?
a: Point-like particles with no attraction to each other
Large particles with strong attraction to each other
Particles at rest in a fixed lattice
Particles that lose energy in every collision
94680.e: In the model, the particles have no volume of their own, interact only through elastic collisions and do not attract each other.
94680.m: Ideal gas particles are point-like and do not attract each other.

94681.q: A gas is compressed to a third of its volume at constant temperature. How does the pressure change?
94681.e: According to Boyle's law, p · V stays the same at constant temperature; a third of the volume means three times the pressure.
94681.m: At constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional.

94682.q: A gas is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C at constant pressure. How does its volume change?
a: It becomes about twelve times larger
It grows by about 10 per cent
94682.e: In kelvin, the temperature rises from 300 K to 600 K, so it doubles; according to Gay-Lussac's law the volume therefore doubles too.
94682.m: With gas laws you must always calculate with the absolute temperature in kelvin.

94683.q: Roughly what pressure does 1 mol of an ideal gas exert in a 10 L container at 300 K?
94683.m: In the gas equation, the volume is given in cubic metres.

94684.q: Which physicist drew up an equation of state for real gases in 1873 that takes into account the volume and attraction of the particles?
94684.e: Van der Waals added two substance-specific constants to the gas equation and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1910.
94684.m: The van der Waals equation describes real gases more accurately than the ideal gas equation.

94685.q: Under which conditions do real gases behave almost like ideal gases?
a: At high temperature and low pressure
At low temperature and high pressure
Only just above their boiling point
At high pressure and any temperature
94685.e: At low pressure the particles are far apart, and at high temperature the attractive forces hardly matter.
94685.m: Real gases behave almost ideally at high temperature and low pressure.

94686.q: In which unit is concentration (amount of substance) usually given in the laboratory?
94686.e: Amount-of-substance concentration is the amount of dissolved substance per volume of solution, so usually moles per litre.
94686.m: Concentration tells you how many moles are dissolved in one litre of solution.

94687.q: 5.85 g of sodium chloride (M about 58.5 g/mol) is dissolved to make 500 mL of solution. What is the concentration?
94687.m: You get the concentration by dividing the amount of substance by the volume of the solution.

94688.q: 100 mL of a solution with c = 2 mol/L is diluted with water to 500 mL. What is the new concentration?
94688.e: c₁ · V₁ = c₂ · V₂, so c₂ = 2 mol/L · 100 mL / 500 mL = 0.4 mol/L.
94688.m: When diluting, the amount of dissolved substance stays the same.

94689.q: How much sodium hydroxide (M about 40 g/mol) do you need for 250 mL of sodium hydroxide solution with c = 0.1 mol/L?
94689.m: Concentration times volume gives the amount of substance needed.

94690.q: What does “0.5 M” on a laboratory bottle mean?
a: 0.5 mol of substance per litre of solution
0.5 mol of substance per kilogram of water
0.5 g of substance per litre of solution
0.5 mol of substance per litre of water
94690.e: The symbol M stands for “molar”, meaning moles per litre of solution; it refers to the volume of the finished solution, not of the solvent.
94690.m: Molar means moles per litre of finished solution.

94691.q: Normal saline contains 9 g of sodium chloride per litre (M about 58.5 g/mol). Roughly what is its concentration?
94691.e: c = 9 g / 58.5 g/mol per litre ≈ 0.154 mol/L.

94692.q: What is the concentration of chloride ions in a calcium chloride solution with c(CaCl₂) = 0.1 mol/L?
94692.e: Each formula unit of CaCl₂ provides two chloride ions, so c(Cl⁻) = 2 · 0.1 mol/L = 0.2 mol/L.
94692.m: The ion concentration depends on how many ions each formula unit produces.

94693.q: You mix 1 L of a solution with c = 1 mol/L and 1 L of the same solution with c = 3 mol/L. What is the concentration of the mixture (with no change in volume)?
94693.e: The total amount, 1 mol + 3 mol = 4 mol in 2 L, gives 2 mol/L.
94693.m: When mixing, you add the amounts of substance and divide by the total volume.

94694.q: How many millilitres of hydrochloric acid with c = 1 mol/L contain 0.05 mol of hydrogen chloride?
94694.e: V = n / c = 0.05 mol / 1 mol/L = 0.05 L = 50 mL.
94694.m: The volume needed is the amount of substance divided by the concentration.

94695.q: What is the point in a titration called at which the amount of standard solution added exactly matches the amount of the substance being tested?
94695.e: At the equivalence point, the reactants have reacted completely in the ratio given by the equation; it is not always at pH 7.
94695.m: At the equivalence point, the substance being tested has just reacted completely.

94696.q: In a titration, in which piece of laboratory equipment is the standard solution?
94696.e: The burette is a finely graduated tube with a tap, clamped upright, from which the standard solution is added drop by drop and the volume read off.
94696.m: The standard solution is dripped in from a burette.

94697.q: 20 mL of hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 25 mL of sodium hydroxide solution (c = 0.1 mol/L). What is the concentration of the hydrochloric acid?
94697.e: n(NaOH) = 0.1 mol/L · 0.025 L = 0.0025 mol; HCl reacts 1 to 1, so c(HCl) = 0.0025 mol / 0.020 L = 0.125 mol/L.
94697.m: In a titration, you work out the unknown concentration from the standard solution used.

94698.q: 10 mL of sulphuric acid is neutralised by 20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution (c = 0.1 mol/L). What is the concentration of the sulphuric acid?
94698.e: n(NaOH) = 0.002 mol; H₂SO₄ gives off two protons, so n(H₂SO₄) = 0.001 mol and c = 0.001 mol / 0.010 L = 0.1 mol/L.
94698.m: With polyprotic acids you must take the ratio in the chemical equation into account.

94699.q: What colour does the indicator phenolphthalein show in a clearly basic solution?
94699.e: Phenolphthalein is colourless in the acidic and neutral range and changes to reddish purple from about pH 8.2.
94699.m: Phenolphthalein turns basic solutions reddish purple.

94700.q: When acetic acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide solution, what is the pH at the point where all the acid has just been neutralised?
94700.e: At that point sodium acetate is present; the acetate ion is a weak base, so the solution is slightly basic.
94700.m: When a weak acid is titrated with a strong base, the end point is in the basic range.

94701.q: In the titration of a weak acid, what is the pH when exactly half of the acid has been neutralised?
a: pH equal to the pKa of the acid
94701.e: At that point the acid and its conjugate base have the same concentration; according to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa.
94701.m: At the half-equivalence point you can read off the pKa of a weak acid directly.

94702.q: What is the burette used for in an acid-base titration?
a: It adds the standard solution in precise amounts and shows the volume used
It measures the pH of the solution
It heats the sample to a fixed temperature
It separates the precipitate from the solution
94702.e: The burette is a glass tube with a scale and a tap. You let the standard solution run in drop by drop and at the end read off how much has been used.
94702.m: The burette measures the volume of standard solution used.

94703.q: Why is no extra indicator needed in a titration with potassium permanganate?
a: The purple solution loses its colour as long as it is being used up
Potassium permanganate glows green at the end point
The solution suddenly turns cloudy at the end point
Manganese is precipitated as a metal at the end point
94703.e: Permanganate ions are intensely purple and are reduced to almost colourless manganese(II) ions; the first lasting pink tinge shows the end point.
94703.m: In redox titrations, potassium permanganate acts as its own indicator.

94704.q: How do you calculate the percentage yield of a reaction?
a: Amount of product obtained divided by the theoretical amount, times 100
Theoretical amount of product divided by the amount obtained, times 100
Mass of product divided by mass of reactants, times 100
Mass of reactants minus mass of product
94704.e: The yield compares how much product is actually formed with the maximum amount possible according to the equation.
94704.m: The yield is the ratio of the amount of product actually obtained to the theoretical amount.

94705.q: In theory a synthesis could produce 50 g of product, but only 40 g is obtained. What is the yield?
94705.m: A yield of 80 per cent means that a fifth of the possible product is missing.

94706.q: Heating 100 g of limestone CaCO₃ (M about 100 g/mol) gives 42 g of quicklime CaO (M about 56 g/mol). What is the yield?
94706.e: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; in theory 1 mol of CaCO₃ gives 56 g of CaO, so 42 g / 56 g · 100 % = 75 %.
94706.m: For the yield, you first work out the theoretical mass of product.

94707.q: Why is the yield in the laboratory almost always below 100 per cent?
a: Because of side reactions and losses during work-up
Because conservation of mass does not always apply
Because catalysts use up some of the product
Because scales always show too much
94707.e: Side reactions, incomplete conversion at equilibrium and losses during filtering or recrystallising reduce the amount obtained.
94707.m: Side reactions and losses during work-up lower the yield.

94708.q: A yield of more than 100 per cent is measured. What is the most likely explanation?
a: The product is still damp or impure
New mass was created in the reaction
94708.e: Because of conservation of mass, more than the theoretical amount is impossible; usually the product still contains solvent or impurities.
94708.m: A yield of over 100 per cent points to an impure or damp product.

94709.q: A synthesis has three steps, each with an 80 per cent yield. Roughly what is the overall yield?
94709.e: The yields are multiplied: 0.8 · 0.8 · 0.8 = 0.512, so about 51 %.
94709.m: In multi-step syntheses, the yields of the individual steps multiply.

94710.q: What does the atom economy of a reaction tell you?
a: What share of the mass of the reactants ends up in the desired product
How quickly the reactants react with each other
How much energy is released per mole of product
How many atoms a product molecule contains
94710.e: Atom economy was introduced by Barry Trost in 1991; reactions without by-products, such as additions, reach 100 per cent.
94710.m: A high atom economy means little waste from by-products.

94711.q: In a 1 to 1 reaction, 0.50 mol of a reactant produces 0.35 mol of product. What is the yield?
94711.e: In theory 0.50 mol would be possible; 0.35 mol / 0.50 mol · 100 % = 70 %.
94711.m: The yield can also be calculated directly with amounts of substance.

94712.q: What is meant by the limiting reactant of a reaction?
a: The reactant that is used up completely first
The reactant with the greatest mass
The substance that speeds up the reaction
94712.e: The limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product that can form; some of the other reactants is left over in excess.
94712.m: The limiting reactant sets the maximum amount of product.

94713.q: For the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, 3 mol of hydrogen and 2 mol of oxygen are available. Which substance is limiting?
94713.e: 3 mol of H₂ only needs 1.5 mol of O₂; so oxygen is in excess and hydrogen is used up first.
94713.m: The limiting substance is the one in shortest supply relative to the chemical equation.

94714.q: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, 2 mol of nitrogen and 3 mol of hydrogen are available. What is the maximum amount of ammonia formed?
94714.e: 3 mol of H₂ reacts with 1 mol of N₂ to form 2 mol of NH₃; hydrogen is limiting and 1 mol of N₂ is left over.
94714.m: The amount of product always depends on the limiting reactant.

94715.q: 56 g of iron (M about 56 g/mol) and 40 g of sulphur (M about 32 g/mol) react to form iron sulphide FeS. How much sulphur is left over?
94715.e: 1 mol of iron reacts with 1 mol of sulphur, which is 32 g; 40 g − 32 g = 8 g of sulphur is left over.
94715.m: Some of the reactant in excess is left over after the reaction.

94716.q: 1 mol of zinc reacts with 1 mol of hydrogen chloride according to Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. What is the maximum amount of hydrogen produced?
94716.e: 1 mol of zinc would need 2 mol of HCl; HCl is limiting, and 1 mol of HCl gives 0.5 mol of H₂.
94716.m: If you overlook the coefficients, it is easy to pick the wrong limiting reactant.

94717.q: Why is a cheap reactant often used in excess in syntheses?
a: So that the expensive reactant reacts as completely as possible
So that the reaction takes in heat
So that less by-product water is formed
So that no catalyst is needed any more
94717.e: If the cheap reactant is in excess, the valuable reactant becomes the limiting reactant and is converted as completely as possible; with equilibria, the excess also shifts the position towards the product.
94717.m: A cheap reactant in excess makes sure the expensive reactant is used well.

94718.q: 16 g of methane (M about 16 g/mol) and 48 g of oxygen (M about 32 g/mol) react according to CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. What is the maximum amount of carbon dioxide (M about 44 g/mol) produced?
94718.e: 1 mol of CH₄ would need 2 mol of O₂, but only 1.5 mol is available; this produces 0.75 mol of CO₂, so 0.75 · 44 g = 33 g.
94718.m: Even in combustion, oxygen can be the limiting reactant.

94719.q: For 2 Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃, 4 mol of aluminium and 3 mol of chlorine are available. How much aluminium is left over?
94719.e: 3 mol of Cl₂ reacts with 2 mol of Al; of the 4 mol of aluminium, 2 mol is left over.
94719.m: The excess is the amount left over once the limiting reactant is used up.

94720.q: What does the law of constant proportions state?
a: A compound always contains its elements in the same mass ratio
The total mass stays the same in a chemical reaction
Gases react in volume ratios of small whole numbers
Two elements can only form one single compound
94720.e: Pure water, for example, always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the same mass ratio, no matter how it was made.
94720.m: A pure compound always has the same composition by mass.

94721.q: Which French chemist formulated the law of constant proportions at the end of the 18th century?
94721.e: Using metal oxides and sulphides, Joseph-Louis Proust showed that their composition stays the same however they are made.
94721.m: Joseph-Louis Proust is regarded as the discoverer of constant mass ratios.

94722.q: Which law states that two elements forming several compounds combine in mass ratios of small whole numbers?
94722.e: Carbon forms CO and CO₂ with oxygen. For the same amount of carbon, CO₂ has exactly twice as much oxygen as CO. John Dalton recognised this rule around 1803.
94722.m: If two elements form several compounds, their masses are in simple number ratios.

94723.q: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water in a mass ratio of about 1 to 8. How much oxygen reacts with 3 g of hydrogen?
94723.e: 3 g · 8 = 24 g of oxygen; this produces 27 g of water.
94723.m: From a fixed mass ratio you can work out how much of the partner is needed.

94724.q: 24 g of magnesium combines with 16 g of oxygen to form magnesium oxide. How much magnesium oxide is formed from 12 g of magnesium?
94724.e: Half the amount of magnesium needs half the amount of oxygen, so 8 g; 12 g + 8 g = 20 g of magnesium oxide.
94724.m: With constant proportions, all the masses change in the same ratio.

94725.q: In a sample of copper(II) sulphide, 6.35 g of copper is combined with 3.21 g of sulphur. How much sulphur is combined in a sample with 19.05 g of copper?
94725.e: 19.05 g is three times 6.35 g, so three times as much sulphur is combined: 3 · 3.21 g = 9.63 g.
94725.m: If you triple the mass of one element in a compound, the mass of its partner triples too.

94726.q: In terms of the law of constant proportions, how does salt water differ from the compound sodium chloride?
a: Salt water varies, sodium chloride has a fixed composition
Salt water has fixed mass ratios, sodium chloride varying ones
Both always have the same fixed mass ratio
94726.e: A mixture like salt water can contain more or less salt; in pure sodium chloride, on the other hand, sodium and chlorine are always in the same mass ratio.
94726.m: Mixtures have a variable composition, compounds a fixed one.

94727.q: What is the empirical formula of glucose C₆H₁₂O₆?
94727.e: The subscripts 6, 12 and 6 can be divided by 6; the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms is 1 to 2 to 1.
94727.m: The empirical formula gives the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms.

94728.q: What is the empirical formula of benzene C₆H₆?
94728.e: Carbon and hydrogen are in the ratio 6 to 6, so 1 to 1; ethyne C₂H₂ also has the same empirical formula.
94728.m: Different substances can have the same empirical formula.

94729.q: What is the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂?
94729.e: The ratio 2 to 2 can be reduced to 1 to 1; the molecular formula H₂O₂, on the other hand, gives the atoms in one molecule.
94729.m: The molecular formula and the empirical formula are not always the same.

94730.q: By mass, a compound consists of 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
94730.m: From the mass percentages you first work out the amounts of substance and then their ratio.

94731.q: By mass, a hydrocarbon consists of 75 % carbon and 25 % hydrogen. What is its empirical formula?
94731.e: In 100 g: 75 / 12 = 6.25 mol C and 25 / 1.008 ≈ 24.8 mol H; the ratio is about 1 to 4.
94731.m: For the empirical formula, you round the ratio of amounts to small whole numbers.

94732.q: By mass, an iron oxide contains 70 % iron (M about 56 g/mol) and 30 % oxygen (M about 16 g/mol). What is its empirical formula?
94732.e: 70 / 56 = 1.25 mol Fe and 30 / 16 = 1.875 mol O; the ratio 1 to 1.5 gives 2 to 3 in whole numbers.
94732.m: If you get a ratio with 0.5, you double both numbers.

94733.q: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and a molar mass of 56 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
94733.e: The CH₂ unit has about 14 g/mol; 56 / 14 = 4, so C₄H₈.
94733.m: With the molar mass, you can find the molecular formula from the empirical formula.

94734.q: Why is only an empirical formula and no molecular formula given for salts such as sodium chloride?
a: An ionic lattice does not consist of individual molecules
Sodium chloride is a gas at room temperature
Salts have no definite molar mass
The ions are too small to count
94734.e: In the crystal, each ion is surrounded by several ions of opposite charge; the formula NaCl only gives the 1 to 1 ratio of the ions.
94734.m: For ionic compounds, the formula only describes the ratio of the ions.

94735.q: Which changes of state make up the Carnot cycle?
94735.e: In the Carnot cycle, heat is taken in and given off at constant temperature; in between, the gas is compressed and expanded without heat exchange.
94735.m: The Carnot cycle alternates between isothermal and adiabatic steps.

94736.q: Who described the ideal cycle of a heat engine in 1824 in the work “Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu”?
94736.e: The French engineer Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot showed that the output of a heat engine depends on the temperature difference.
94736.m: In 1824 Sadi Carnot founded the theory of heat engines.

94737.q: What is the efficiency of the Carnot cycle with the upper temperature T_w and the lower temperature T_k (in kelvin)?
94737.e: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the two absolute temperatures; the larger the difference, the higher the efficiency.
94737.m: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the absolute temperatures of the two heat reservoirs.

94738.q: What temperature would the cold reservoir need to have for a Carnot engine to reach an efficiency of 100 %?
94738.e: Only if T_k were 0 K would the fraction T_k / T_w disappear; but absolute zero cannot be reached.
94738.m: An efficiency of 100 per cent is impossible for heat engines.

94739.q: In the clockwise Carnot cycle, which step follows directly after the isothermal expansion?
94739.e: After taking in heat at high temperature, the gas continues to expand without heat exchange and cools down to the low temperature; then come isothermal and adiabatic compression.
94739.m: In the Carnot cycle, the gas cools from the high to the low temperature during the adiabatic expansion.

94740.q: Why does no real heat engine reach the Carnot efficiency?
a: Real processes such as friction and heat conduction are irreversible
Real engines work with too little working gas
The Carnot efficiency only applies to steam
Real engines do not use temperature differences
94740.e: The Carnot cycle is completely reversible; friction, heat transfer across finite temperature differences and flow losses produce entropy in real engines.
94740.m: Irreversible losses keep real engines below the Carnot efficiency.

94741.q: What does the area enclosed by the cycle in the p-V diagram represent?
a: The internal energy of the gas
94741.e: Work equals the integral of p with respect to V; over a closed cycle, the enclosed area is the net work.
94741.m: In the p-V diagram, the area enclosed by a cycle is the work gained.

94742.q: Which measure increases the Carnot efficiency of an engine?
a: Filling more working gas into the cylinder
94742.e: A higher upper temperature or a lower lower temperature makes the fraction T_k / T_w smaller and so increases the efficiency.
94742.m: A larger temperature difference allows a higher efficiency.

94743.q: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K. What is its efficiency?
94743.m: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the two absolute temperatures.

94744.q: How is the efficiency of a machine defined?
a: Useful power divided by power supplied
Power supplied divided by useful power
Power lost divided by useful power
94744.e: Efficiency η compares the benefit with the input and always lies between 0 and 1, or 0 and 100 %.
94744.m: Efficiency is the ratio of benefit to input.

94745.q: An engine delivers 45 kW of mechanical power and takes in 150 kW with the fuel. What is its efficiency?
94745.m: To get the efficiency, divide the power delivered by the power taken in.

94746.q: A drive consists of a motor with 90 % efficiency and a gearbox with 80 % efficiency. What is the overall efficiency?
94746.e: For components connected one after another, the efficiencies are multiplied: 0.9 · 0.8 = 0.72.
94746.m: Efficiencies of components in series are multiplied.

94747.q: Roughly what share of the electrical energy in a traditional incandescent bulb becomes visible light?
94747.e: By far the largest part of the energy is given off as heat; only a few per cent becomes visible light.
94747.m: An incandescent bulb is more of a heater than a light source.

94748.q: An engine takes in 200 kW of fuel power and has an efficiency of 35 %. How much power is lost as waste heat?
94748.e: Useful power 0.35 · 200 kW = 70 kW; the remaining 200 kW − 70 kW = 130 kW becomes heat.
94748.m: What a machine does not deliver as useful power mostly becomes waste heat.

94749.q: Why does a combined heat and power plant achieve a particularly high fuel utilisation?
a: The waste heat is used for heating
It burns the fuel without oxygen
It produces no waste heat at all
94749.e: In combined heat and power, the waste heat is used as well as the electricity, for example for a district heating network; in total up to about 90 % of the fuel energy can be used.
94749.m: Combined heat and power uses electricity and waste heat at the same time.

94750.q: What does “well-to-wheel” efficiency describe for vehicles?
a: The chain from the energy source to the wheel
Only the efficiency of the engine
Only the losses in the gearbox
The rolling resistance of the tyres
94750.e: Well-to-wheel covers extraction or production, transport, storage and conversion in the vehicle; tank-to-wheel only looks at the part in the vehicle.
94750.m: Well-to-wheel looks at the whole energy chain from the source to the wheel.

94751.q: Roughly what efficiency do large hydroelectric power stations reach when turning the potential energy of water into electricity?
94751.e: The turbines and generators of large hydroelectric power stations work with very small losses, because no heat has to be turned into work.
94751.m: Hydroelectric power stations turn energy into electricity with very small losses.

94752.q: Why is the efficiency of thermal power stations basically lower than that of hydroelectric power stations?
a: Heat can only partly be turned into work
Steam turbines turn more slowly than water turbines
Thermal power stations have no generator
Fuels contain less energy than water
94752.e: Every heat engine has to give off waste heat; hydropower, on the other hand, converts mechanical energy directly.
94752.m: When heat is turned into work, part of it is always lost as waste heat.

94753.q: In what order do the four strokes of a four-stroke petrol engine take place?
94753.e: First the piston draws in the mixture and compresses it. Then the spark plug fires and the burning gas pushes the piston down. Finally, the exhaust gases are pushed out.
94753.m: The four-stroke engine works with intake, compression, power and exhaust.

94754.q: What does the efficiency of the ideal Otto cycle mainly depend on?
94754.e: In the ideal Otto cycle, η = 1 − ε^(1-κ); the more the mixture is compressed, the higher the efficiency.
94754.m: Higher compression improves the efficiency of a petrol engine.

94755.q: Why does a real petrol engine reach a much lower efficiency than the ideal Otto cycle?
a: Because of heat losses, friction and incomplete combustion
Because the fuel contains too much energy
Because the engine has too few cylinders
Because the spark plug uses too much electricity
94755.e: The ideal cycle has no losses. In a real engine, heat is lost through the cylinder walls and cooling, pistons and bearings rub, and not everything burns. Real petrol engines reach about 25 to 40 per cent.
94755.m: The ideal Otto efficiency is far above that of a real engine.

94756.q: What is meant by “knocking” in a petrol engine?
a: Uncontrolled self-ignition of parts of the mixture
Too little oil in the sump
94756.e: When an engine knocks, parts of the mixture ignite by themselves before the flame front reaches them; the pressure peaks can damage the pistons and cylinder head.
94756.m: Knocking is harmful, uncontrolled combustion in a petrol engine.

94757.q: Which substance has an octane number of 100 by definition?
94757.e: The octane number measures resistance to knocking; isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) is given the value 100, n-heptane the value 0.
94757.m: The octane number compares a fuel with a mixture of isooctane and n-heptane.

94758.q: Which three pollutants does a three-way catalytic converter convert?
94758.e: Carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons are oxidised, while nitrogen oxides are at the same time reduced to nitrogen.
94758.m: The three-way catalytic converter breaks down three groups of pollutants at once.

94759.q: To which air ratio λ does the lambda sensor regulate a petrol engine with a three-way catalytic converter?
94759.e: Only with exactly the stoichiometric amount of air does the three-way catalytic converter work best for all pollutants.
94759.m: A petrol engine with a catalytic converter runs with exactly the stoichiometric amount of air.

94760.q: Roughly how much air is needed to burn 1 kg of petrol completely?
94760.e: The stoichiometric air to fuel ratio of petrol is about 14.7 to 1 (by mass).
94760.m: For one kilogram of petrol an engine needs almost fifteen kilograms of air.

94761.q: How is the fuel ignited in a diesel engine?
a: By the heat of the highly compressed air
By a spark from the spark plug
By an open flame in the cylinder
By friction of the piston against the wall
94761.e: When compressed, the air heats up to several hundred degrees. The injected diesel ignites in it by itself.
94761.m: The diesel engine is a compression-ignition engine.

94762.q: In which decade did Rudolf Diesel build his first working engine?
94762.e: Rudolf Diesel applied for his patent in 1892 and got the first working engine running at the Augsburg machine works in 1897.
94762.m: The diesel engine was created in the 1890s.

94763.q: What compression ratio do car diesel engines typically have?
94763.e: The air has to be compressed so much that it becomes hot enough for the injected fuel to ignite by itself.
94763.m: Diesel engines compress the air much more than petrol engines.

94764.q: What does the cetane number of a diesel fuel indicate?
94764.e: A high cetane number means that the fuel ignites by itself quickly after injection; this makes the engine run more smoothly.
94764.m: The cetane number describes how easily diesel fuel ignites.

94765.q: Which exhaust system reduces nitrogen oxides in diesel exhaust using a solution of urea in water?
94765.e: In selective catalytic reduction (SCR), urea produces ammonia, which converts the nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water.
94765.m: An SCR catalytic converter breaks down nitrogen oxides with ammonia from urea.

a: A shared high-pressure reservoir supplies all injectors
Each cylinder has its own mechanical pump
The fuel is sprayed in before the inlet valve
The fuel flows in by gravity alone
94766.e: A pump keeps the fuel in a shared line (rail) at very high pressure; electronically controlled injectors inject several times per working cycle.
94766.m: With common rail, the injection pressure is always there, whatever the engine speed.

94767.q: Roughly what efficiency do large, slow-running two-stroke marine diesel engines reach?
94767.e: Large marine diesels are among the most efficient heat engines; such engines are developed in Winterthur, among other places.
94767.m: Large marine diesel engines turn more than half of the fuel energy into work.

94768.q: Why is a diesel engine usually more economical than a petrol engine at part load?
a: It does not throttle the intake air
It always runs at top speed
94768.e: The diesel engine controls its power through the amount of fuel injected; in a petrol engine, the throttle valve causes gas exchange losses at part load.
94768.m: A diesel engine controls its power through the amount of fuel instead of a throttle valve.

94769.q: How many turns of the crankshaft does one complete working cycle of a four-stroke engine take?
94769.e: Each stroke corresponds to one piston stroke, that is half a turn; four strokes make two turns or 720 degrees.
94769.m: A four-stroke engine needs two crankshaft turns for one working cycle.

94770.q: What is valve overlap in a four-stroke engine?
a: The inlet and exhaust valves are open at the same time for a short while
Two valves touch each other in the cylinder head
One valve opens twice per stroke
The exhaust valve stays open permanently
94770.e: At the end of the exhaust stroke, the inlet valve already opens before the exhaust valve closes; the outflowing exhaust gases help to draw in fresh mixture.
94770.m: With valve overlap, inlet and exhaust are briefly open at the same time.

94771.q: In which stroke does a four-stroke engine deliver work to the crankshaft?
94771.e: Only in the power stroke do the hot combustion gases push the piston down; the other strokes use energy from the flywheel.
94771.m: Only one of the four strokes delivers work.

94772.q: A four-cylinder engine has an 80 mm bore and a 90 mm stroke. Roughly what is its engine capacity?
94772.e: Per cylinder: π/4 · (8 cm)² · 9 cm ≈ 452 cm³; times 4 gives about 1810 cm³.
94772.m: Engine capacity is piston area times stroke times number of cylinders.

94773.q: An engine delivers a torque of 200 Nm at 3000 revolutions per minute. Roughly what is its power?
94773.m: The power of an engine is torque times angular velocity.

94774.q: How often does each cylinder of a two-stroke engine deliver a power stroke?
94774.e: In a two-stroke engine, gas exchange and work happen at the same time, controlled by ports in the cylinder wall.
94774.m: A two-stroke engine fires in every cylinder on every turn.

94775.q: What is an exhaust turbocharger on a four-stroke engine for?
a: It compresses the intake air using energy from the exhaust
It cools the exhaust before the catalytic converter
94775.e: A turbine in the exhaust flow drives a compressor; more air in the cylinder allows more fuel and therefore more power from a small engine capacity.
94775.m: A turbocharger uses exhaust energy to force more air into the engine.

94776.q: When does the spark plug of a petrol engine typically fire?
a: In the middle of the intake stroke
94776.e: Because combustion takes a little time, ignition happens before top dead centre (ignition advance), so that the peak pressure is reached shortly afterwards.
94776.m: Ignition happens just before the piston is at the very top.

a: In aircraft engines and power stations
94777.e: Aircraft jet engines are gas turbines. In power stations, gas turbines drive generators, often combined with a steam turbine.
94777.m: Gas turbines power aircraft and generators.

94778.q: In what order does the air flow through the main parts of a gas turbine?
94778.e: The air is compressed, heated in the combustion chamber by burning fuel and then expanded in the turbine, which also drives the compressor.
94778.m: A gas turbine compresses, heats and expands the air, in that order.

94779.q: Which Swiss company built the first gas turbine for generating electricity in Neuchâtel in 1939?
94779.e: The 4 MW plant by BBC from Baden supplied emergency power for the city of Neuchâtel; today it is recognised as a historic engineering landmark and stands in Birr.
94779.m: The first gas turbine for generating electricity came from Switzerland in 1939.

94780.q: What electrical efficiency do modern combined-cycle gas and steam power stations reach?
94780.e: By combining a gas turbine and a steam turbine, modern plants reach efficiencies of over 60 %.
94780.m: Combined-cycle power stations are among the most efficient thermal power stations.

94781.q: How does a combined-cycle gas and steam power station work?
a: The hot exhaust gases of the gas turbine produce steam for a steam turbine
Gas and steam are burnt together in one turbine
The steam turbine supplies fuel for the gas turbine
Gas is cooled with steam and then stored
94781.e: The exhaust from the gas turbine is still about 600 °C hot; in a heat recovery boiler it produces steam, which generates extra electricity.
94781.m: A combined-cycle power station uses the waste heat of the gas turbine for a second turbine.

94782.q: Why are the front turbine blades of modern gas turbines cooled with air from inside?
a: The hot gas is hotter than the melting point of the material
So that the blades turn faster
So that there is less noise
So that the fuel is preheated
94782.e: In modern plants, the turbine inlet temperature is well over 1300 °C; only cooling and protective coatings keep the blades intact.
94782.m: Without cooling, the hottest turbine blades would melt.

94783.q: What material are the hottest turbine blades of modern gas turbines usually made of?
94783.e: Nickel-based superalloys, often cast as a single crystal, keep their strength even at very high temperatures.
94783.m: Nickel-based superalloys can withstand extreme temperatures.

94784.q: Why is the efficiency of a combined-cycle gas and steam power station higher than that of a gas turbine alone?
a: The waste heat of the gas turbine is also used for a steam turbine
Because steam contains more energy than gas
Because the plant burns less fuel than the energy it produces
Because the steam turbine runs on solar energy
94784.e: The exhaust gases of a gas turbine are still about 600 °C hot. A combined-cycle power station uses this heat to make steam for a second turbine, reaching an efficiency of over 60 %.
94784.m: A combined-cycle power station uses the waste heat a second time.

94785.q: Which physical principle is the thrust of a jet engine based on?
94785.e: The engine accelerates air and combustion gases backwards; according to Newton's third law, an equal force acts forwards.
94785.m: A jet engine produces thrust by accelerating gas backwards.

94786.q: Which aircraft made the first flight with a turbojet engine in 1939?
94786.e: The He 178, with an engine by Hans von Ohain, flew in Rostock on 27 August 1939.
94786.m: The world's first jet aircraft flew in 1939.

94787.q: Which British engineer applied for a patent for a turbojet engine in 1930?
94787.e: Frank Whittle developed the turbojet engine in Great Britain largely independently of the work in Germany.
94787.m: Frank Whittle is regarded as one of the inventors of the jet engine.

94788.q: What does the bypass ratio of a turbofan engine indicate?
a: Air flowing past the core divided by air flowing through the core
Fuel divided by air taken in
Fan speed divided by turbine speed
94788.e: In modern airliners, many times more air flows through the outer duct past the core engine.
94788.m: The bypass ratio compares the air in the bypass flow with the air in the core.

94789.q: Why are turbofans with a high bypass ratio more economical?
a: Accelerating a lot of air a little is more efficient than a little air a lot
Because they do without a combustion chamber
Because the fan preheats the fuel
Because they only produce thrust at high altitude
94789.e: Thrust is mass flow times increase in speed, but the energy lost in the exhaust jet grows with the square of the speed; a slow, wide jet is therefore more efficient and quieter.
94789.m: A large, slow jet of air produces thrust with less energy loss.

94790.q: Which engine has no mechanical compressor and only works at high flight speed?
94790.e: In a ramjet, the air is compressed in the intake by the forward motion alone; when standing still it produces no thrust.
94790.m: A ramjet needs the airflow from forward motion instead of a compressor.

94791.q: What does an afterburner do on a fighter jet engine?
a: More thrust with much higher fuel consumption
Cooler exhaust gases behind the engine
94791.e: Behind the turbine, extra fuel is sprayed into the exhaust flow, which is still rich in oxygen, and burnt; this greatly increases the thrust for a short time.
94791.m: An afterburner increases thrust at the cost of high fuel consumption.

94792.q: An engine accelerates 50 kg of air per second from 250 m/s to 650 m/s. Roughly what is the thrust (ignoring the mass of the fuel)?
94792.e: F = mass flow · change in speed = 50 kg/s · (650 − 250) m/s = 20,000 N.
94792.m: Thrust is mass flow times increase in speed.

94793.q: Which law requires every heat engine to give off part of its heat to colder surroundings?
94793.e: According to the second law, heat cannot be completely turned into work; part of it must flow as waste heat to a colder reservoir.
94793.m: No heat engine can work without waste heat.

94794.q: What do you call an imaginary machine that turns heat from just one heat reservoir completely into work?
a: Perpetual motion machine of the second kind
Perpetual motion machine of the first kind
94794.e: Such a machine would conserve energy, but it would deliver work without a temperature difference; that contradicts all experience and is impossible.
94794.m: A perpetual motion machine of the second kind cannot exist.

94795.q: A heat engine takes in 1000 J of heat per cycle and gives off 650 J of waste heat. How much work does it do?
94795.e: According to the law of conservation of energy, W = Q_in − Q_out = 1000 J − 650 J = 350 J; so the efficiency is 35 %.
94795.m: The work is the heat taken in minus the heat given off.

a: Heat comes from outside, and the working gas stays sealed in
Fuel is burnt directly in the cylinder
94796.e: The engine, patented by Robert Stirling in 1816, heats a sealed gas from outside, for example with solar heat or a flame, and cools it on the other side.
94796.m: A Stirling engine is a heat engine with an external heat supply.

94797.q: Which machine in a steam power station turns the energy of the hot steam into a rotating movement?
94797.e: The steam flows through the turbine at high pressure and makes it turn. The turbine drives the generator; afterwards the steam turns back into water in the condenser.
94797.m: In a steam power station, the steam drives a turbine.

94798.q: What is the cooling tower of a power station such as Gösgen or Leibstadt for?
a: It releases the waste heat from the condenser into the air
It cools the reactor directly in an emergency
It stores steam for the night
It filters radioactive substances out of the air
94798.e: The steam from the turbine has to be turned back into liquid in the condenser; the waste heat released reaches the surroundings via the cooling water and the cooling tower.
94798.m: The cooling tower removes the unavoidable waste heat of a thermal power station.

94799.q: Which physicist introduced the term “entropy” in 1865?
94799.e: Rudolf Clausius formulated the second law and coined the term entropy from the Greek word for “transformation”.
94799.m: Rudolf Clausius gave entropy its name.

94800.q: Where does a heat engine get its work from?
a: From a flow of heat from the hot to the cold reservoir
From the mass of the fuel burnt
From the air pressure of the surroundings alone
From the rotation of the Earth
94800.e: Part of the heat that flows from the hot to the cold reservoir is turned into mechanical work.
94800.m: A heat engine taps into a flow of heat between two temperatures.

94801.q: In which part of a compression refrigerator does the refrigerant take in heat from the cold compartment?
94801.e: In the evaporator, the refrigerant boils at low pressure and low temperature and draws heat from its surroundings.
94801.m: In the evaporator, the refrigerant takes in heat as it boils.

94802.q: What job does the expansion valve do in a refrigerator?
a: It lowers the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant
It raises the pressure of the refrigerant
It gives off heat to the surroundings
It filters dirt out of the refrigerant
94802.e: As the liquid refrigerant flows through the narrow point, it expands; its pressure and boiling temperature drop sharply.
94802.m: The expansion valve lets the refrigerant expand to low pressure.

94803.q: A fridge removes 300 W of heat from the inside and takes in 100 W of electrical power. How much heat does it give off into the kitchen?
94803.e: According to the law of conservation of energy, it gives off the heat removed plus the work supplied: 300 W + 100 W = 400 W.
94803.m: A fridge gives off more heat than it removes from the inside.

94804.q: When does a refrigerator or heat pump work particularly efficiently?
a: When the temperature difference between the cold and warm sides is small
When the temperature difference is as large as possible
When the refrigerant is as warm as possible
When the compressor runs as slowly as possible
94804.e: The less far the heat has to be “pumped up”, the less electrical work the machine needs per amount of heat. That is why a heat pump with underfloor heating is more efficient than one with hot radiators.
94804.m: The smaller the temperature difference, the more efficiently a refrigerator works.

94805.q: Which international agreement of 1987 led to the ban on CFC refrigerants?
94805.e: CFCs destroy the ozone layer; the Montreal Protocol governs the worldwide phase-out of ozone-depleting substances.
94805.m: The Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer.

94806.q: Which natural refrigerant is used today in most household fridges in Europe?
94806.e: Isobutane (R600a) does not damage the ozone layer and has a very low global warming potential; because it is flammable, appliances contain only a few grams.
94806.m: Modern household fridges mostly work with isobutane.

94807.q: Which two physicists jointly patented a fridge with no moving parts in 1930?
94807.e: The Einstein-Szilard refrigerator is an absorption refrigerator that runs on heat alone and needs no compressor.
94807.m: Even Albert Einstein worked on refrigeration technology.

94808.q: Why doesn't a kitchen get cooler if you leave the fridge door open?
a: It gives off more heat at the back than it removes at the front
The kitchen walls store the cold
94808.e: The fridge only pumps heat from the front to the back into the same room and adds the electrical energy as extra heat; overall the room gets warmer.
94808.m: A refrigerator in a closed room heats it up overall.

94809.q: What characterises a series hybrid drive?
a: The combustion engine only drives a generator
Both motors always drive the wheels together
The vehicle runs only on hydrogen
The electric motor only serves as a starter
94809.e: In a series hybrid, the wheels are driven only electrically; the combustion engine just produces electricity.
94809.m: In a series hybrid, the vehicle always drives electrically.

94810.q: What distinguishes a plug-in hybrid from an ordinary full hybrid?
a: Its battery can be charged from the mains
94810.e: Plug-in hybrids have a larger battery that is charged from a socket and can often drive a few dozen kilometres on electricity alone.
94810.m: A plug-in hybrid can be charged from a socket.

94811.q: What can a mild hybrid with a 48-volt electrical system usually not do?
a: Drive longer distances on electricity alone
Support the engine when pulling away
Switch the engine off at traffic lights
94811.e: The small electric motor of a mild hybrid only supports the combustion engine; its power and battery are too small for purely electric driving.
94811.m: A mild hybrid supports the combustion engine but can hardly drive on electricity alone.

94812.q: Which car came onto the market in Japan in 1997 as the first mass-produced hybrid car?
94812.e: The Prius combined a petrol engine with two electric machines and did a lot to spread hybrid technology.
94812.m: The first mass-produced hybrid car appeared in Japan in 1997.

94813.q: In a power-split hybrid, which type of gear divides the engine power between the wheels and the generator?
94813.e: The sun gear, planet carrier and ring gear are connected to the generator, combustion engine and drive; the whole thing works like a continuously variable transmission.
94813.m: A planetary gear divides the power in a power-split hybrid.

94814.q: What happens to the braking energy in a hybrid car?
a: The electric motor turns it into electricity for the battery
It is fed into the tank as heat
It drives the air conditioning directly
94814.e: When braking, the electric motor works as a generator. The electricity gained is stored in the battery and used again the next time the car pulls away. This is called regenerative braking.

94815.q: Which designer built one of the first hybrid cars, the “Semper Vivus”, around 1900?
94815.e: In the Lohner-Porsche “Semper Vivus”, combustion engines drove generators that supplied electricity to wheel hub motors.
94815.m: Hybrid cars already existed around the year 1900.

94816.q: When does a full hybrid save a particularly large amount of fuel compared with a pure combustion-engine car?
a: In town traffic with frequent pulling away and braking
On long motorway journeys at a steady speed
At full throttle with a trailer on a hill
At top speed on a racetrack
94816.e: In town, a hybrid can often pull away electrically, store braking energy and run the combustion engine in its efficient range.
94816.m: Hybrids show their strengths above all in stop-and-go traffic.

94817.q: What efficiency do the electric motors of electric cars typically reach?
94817.e: Electric motors turn electrical energy into motion with very small losses, much better than combustion engines.
94817.m: Electric motors are much more efficient than combustion engines.

94818.q: What advantage do lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have over batteries with a nickel manganese cobalt cathode?
a: They need no cobalt and last a very long time
They have a much higher energy density
They are lighter per kilowatt hour
They can only be charged with alternating current
94818.e: LFP cells are cheaper, more thermally stable and can withstand many charging cycles, but they store a little less energy per kilogram.
94818.m: LFP batteries are robust and do without cobalt.

94819.q: An electric car uses 18 kWh per 100 km and has 72 kWh of usable battery capacity. Roughly how far can it go?
94819.e: 72 kWh / 18 kWh per 100 km = 4, so 400 km.
94819.m: The range is the battery capacity divided by the consumption.

94820.q: Roughly how long does it take to charge 55 kWh with an 11 kW wallbox (ignoring losses)?
94820.m: The charging time is the amount of energy divided by the charging power.

94821.q: Why do electric cars charge much more slowly at fast chargers once they reach about 80 per cent?
a: The battery management lowers the current to protect the cells
The charging station switches to alternating current at 80 per cent
The battery is already too cold by then
Electricity is more expensive above 80 per cent
94821.e: At a high state of charge, the cell voltage rises; to avoid overcharging, heating and ageing, the final part of charging is done with a falling current.
94821.m: The last few per cent of a battery are charged more slowly to protect it.

94822.q: How much energy is 1 kWh in megajoules?

94823.q: Which type of motor is used in many electric cars because it works very efficiently with permanent magnets in the rotor?
94823.e: Permanent magnet synchronous motors have high efficiency and high power density; induction motors are also used.
94823.m: Many electric cars run on permanent magnet synchronous motors.

94824.q: Which component in an electric car converts the battery's direct current into three-phase current for the motor?
94824.e: The inverter uses power semiconductors to produce three-phase current with the right frequency and voltage, and so controls speed and torque.
94824.m: The inverter turns battery current into three-phase current for the motor.

94825.q: An electric car needs 15 kWh per 100 km. How many litres of petrol is that equivalent to in energy terms (1 L of petrol is about 9 kWh)?
94825.e: 15 kWh / 9 kWh per litre ≈ 1.7 L; a comparable petrol car usually needs over 5 L, because its engine produces a lot of waste heat.
94825.m: In energy terms, an electric car needs only a fraction of what a petrol car needs.

94826.q: What is meant by regenerative braking in vehicles?
a: Recovering braking energy with the motor as a generator
Charging the battery with solar collectors
Feeding exhaust gas back into the intake
94826.e: When braking, the electric motor works as a generator; the kinetic energy is turned into electricity and stored in the battery.
94826.m: With regenerative braking, braking energy is turned back into electrical energy.

94827.q: A car weighing 1500 kg is travelling at 72 km/h. What is its kinetic energy?
94827.m: For kinetic energy you have to use the speed in metres per second.

94828.q: When braking, a car recovers 50 % of 360 kJ of kinetic energy. How much is that in kilowatt hours?
94828.m: A single braking manoeuvre recovers only a little energy, but many add up.

94829.q: What does “one-pedal driving” mean in electric cars?
a: When you release the accelerator, the car brakes strongly through regeneration
The car no longer has a brake pedal
The car only drives with cruise control
94829.e: When you take your foot off the accelerator, the motor slows the car down as a generator so strongly that you rarely need the friction brake in everyday driving.
94829.m: In one-pedal driving, you control speeding up and braking with the same pedal.

94830.q: Where do electric locomotives of the SBB (Swiss Federal Railways) usually send the energy gained during electric braking?
a: Into a water tank for heating
Through the rails into the ground
94830.e: Modern locomotives feed the braking energy back into the overhead line as electricity, where other trains can use it.
94830.m: Braking electric locomotives can supply electricity for other trains.

94831.q: What was the name of the system introduced in Formula 1 in 2009 that stores braking energy and releases it at the push of a button?
94831.e: KERS stands for Kinetic Energy Recovery System; it was later developed into the MGU-K of the hybrid power units.
94831.m: Motor racing also uses the recovery of braking energy.

94832.q: Why can an electric car with a full battery hardly use regenerative braking?
a: The battery cannot take in any more energy
94832.e: If the battery is full, further charging would overload the cells; the car then brakes more with the friction brake.
94832.m: A full battery can no longer store braking energy.

94833.q: Which vehicle in a quarry near Biel recovers more energy when driving downhill loaded than it needs to drive uphill?
a: A hybrid tractor with a trailer
94833.e: The eDumper drives uphill empty and downhill heavily loaded; the energy recovered is more than it uses, so it does not need to be charged externally.
94833.m: If you drive downhill heavily loaded, regenerative braking can gain more energy than you use going uphill.

94834.q: On which route does an electric car recover a particularly large amount of energy through regenerative braking?
a: On a long descent from an Alpine pass
At a steady speed on a flat motorway
When standing still in a traffic jam
Driving at full throttle on a racetrack
94834.e: On a descent from a pass, potential energy is released over a long time, which the motor can feed back into the battery as a generator.
94834.m: Downhill drives are especially good for regenerative braking.

94835.q: Which logic gate only gives a 1 when all inputs are 1?
94835.e: The AND gate only outputs 1 when all inputs are 1. Otherwise the output is 0.
94835.m: An AND gate needs all ones to output a one.

94836.q: Which gate outputs 0 for the inputs 1 and 1, but 1 for 1 and 0?
94836.e: XOR (exclusive or) gives 1 when exactly one input is 1. If both are 1, the output is 0.
94836.m: XOR is true when the two inputs differ.

94837.q: With which gates alone can every Boolean function be built?
94837.e: NAND and NOR are functionally complete: from them alone you can build NOT, AND and OR and therefore any switching function.
94837.m: NAND and NOR are called universal gates.

94838.q: How many rows does the truth table of a gate with three inputs have?
94838.e: Each input can be 0 or 1, so there are 2 to the power of 3, that is 8, combinations.
94838.m: With n inputs, a truth table has 2 to the power of n rows.

94839.q: What does a NOR gate output when both inputs are 0?
94839.e: NOR is a negated OR. 0 OR 0 gives 0, and its negation is 1.
94839.m: A NOR gate only outputs 1 when all inputs are 0.

94840.q: According to De Morgan's laws, which expression is equivalent to NOT(A AND B)?
94840.e: De Morgan states that the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations.
94840.m: When negating, AND becomes OR and each part is negated.

94841.q: What are the logic gates in today's computer chips made of?
94841.e: Modern chips contain billions of tiny transistors in CMOS technology. Early computers still built their gates from relays or valves.
94841.m: Logic gates today are made of transistors.

94842.q: When does an XNOR gate with two inputs give a 1?
a: When both inputs are the same
94842.e: XNOR is the negated XOR. It therefore reports equality: 0 and 0 as well as 1 and 1 give 1.
94842.m: The XNOR gate works like an equality checker for two bits.

94843.q: Which two outputs does a half adder have?
94843.e: A half adder adds two bits and outputs the sum bit and the carry bit.
94843.m: The half adder gives a sum bit and a carry bit.

94844.q: Which gate produces the sum bit in a half adder?
94844.e: The sum bit is 1 when exactly one of the two bits is 1. That matches the XOR function exactly.
94844.m: The sum of a half adder comes from an XOR.

94845.q: Which gate produces the carry bit in a half adder?
94845.e: A carry only happens with 1 plus 1. That is exactly the AND of the two inputs.
94845.m: The carry of a half adder comes from an AND.

94846.q: What does a half adder lack compared with a full adder?
a: An input for the carry from the previous digit
An output for the sum bit
An input for the sign bit
94846.e: The full adder has three inputs: two bits and the incoming carry. The half adder lacks this carry input.
94846.m: Only the full adder can process a carry from the previous digit.

94847.q: Which components are enough to build a full adder?
a: Two half adders and an OR gate
One half adder and a NOT gate
Three half adders without other gates
94847.e: The first half adder adds the two bits and the second adds the incoming carry. An OR combines the two partial carries.
94847.m: Two half adders and an OR together make a full adder.

94848.q: What does a half adder output when both inputs are 1?
94848.e: 1 plus 1 is 10 in binary. So the sum bit is 0 and the carry is 1.

94849.q: An adder passes the carry on from digit to digit. Why does it become slow with many bits?
a: Each digit has to wait for the carry from the previous one
Each digit needs its own clock
The sum bits are calculated twice
It can only add even numbers
94849.e: The carry runs through all the digits like a wave. The more bits, the longer it takes until the last sum bit is fixed.
94849.m: A carry that is passed along slows down wide adders.

94850.q: What does the binary addition 0111 + 0001 give?
94850.e: 1 + 1 gives 0 with a carry of 1. The carry runs on through all three ones until it creates a 1 in the fourth place: 1000.
94850.m: A carry can run on over several digits.

94851.q: What is a register in a processor?
a: A very fast storage place directly in the processor
An area on the hard disk for file names
A list of all installed programs
A part of main memory for graphics data
94851.e: Registers are small memory cells in the processor that the arithmetic logic unit can access without delay.
94851.m: Registers are a computer's fastest memory.

94852.q: What does the program counter store?
a: The address of the next instruction
The number of instructions already carried out
The result of the last calculation
The number of the running process
94852.e: The program counter points to the memory address from which the next machine instruction is fetched. A jump changes its value.
94852.m: The program counter always knows where the program goes next.

94853.q: What does the instruction register contain?
a: The list of all instructions in a program
94853.e: After fetching, the instruction is loaded into the instruction register, where the control unit decodes it.
94853.m: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded.

94854.q: In simple processors, what is the register called where the results of the arithmetic logic unit end up?
94854.e: In accumulator machines, the accumulator is an operand and also the target of most arithmetic operations.
94854.m: The accumulator collects the results of calculations.

94855.q: What does the stack pointer point to?
a: The current end of the stack
The start of the program code
94855.e: The stack pointer holds the address of the top of the stack. PUSH and POP change it automatically.
94855.m: The stack pointer marks the top of the stack.

94856.q: When is the zero flag set in the status register?
a: When the result of an operation is zero
When a division by zero is attempted
94856.e: The zero flag shows that the last result was 0. Conditional jumps such as “jump if equal” use it.
94856.m: The zero flag reports a result of zero.

94857.q: What does 64 bit mean for a processor?
a: It has 64 GB of main memory
94857.e: In a 64-bit processor, the general registers hold 64 bits. This lets it handle large numbers and a great deal of main memory directly.
94857.m: A processor's bit width is the width of its registers.

94858.q: What does the carry flag show after an addition?
a: A carry out of the most significant bit
94858.e: The carry flag is set when, with unsigned numbers, a carry goes beyond the width of the register.
94858.m: The carry flag reports a carry beyond the top bit.

94859.q: What does the abbreviation RISC stand for?
