a: The catalyst and the reaction mixture are in different phases.
The catalyst and the reaction mixture are dissolved in the same phase.
96152.e: Typically there is a solid catalyst on whose surface gases or liquids react. In homogeneous catalysis, everything is dissolved in one phase.
96152.m: In heterogeneous catalysis, substances react on the surface of a catalyst in a different phase.

96153.q: In what order do the steps on a solid catalyst take place?
96153.e: First the reactants bind to the surface, they react there, and then the products come off again. This frees the surface for new particles.
96153.m: Attach, react and detach are the three steps of surface catalysis.

96154.q: Which metals does a three-way catalytic converter in a car mainly contain?
96154.e: The precious metals are finely spread over a ceramic honeycomb structure. This creates a very large active surface.
96154.m: Platinum, palladium and rhodium do the work in a car's catalytic converter.

96155.q: Which three groups of pollutants does a three-way catalytic converter break down at the same time?
96155.e: CO and hydrocarbons are oxidised to CO₂ and water, and nitrogen oxides are reduced to nitrogen. For this, the air-fuel ratio must be exactly right.
96155.m: The three-way catalytic converter oxidises and reduces at the same time.

96156.q: Why must a car with a catalytic converter not be filled with leaded petrol?
a: Lead poisons the active surface of the catalyst.
Lead makes the catalyst too hot.
96156.e: Lead compounds settle on the precious metals and block the active sites. This is called a catalyst poison.
96156.m: Catalyst poisons block the active sites on the surface.

96157.q: Which catalyst oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ in the contact process?
96157.e: V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide, from which sulphuric acid is made. Platinum used to be used for this.
96157.m: In the contact process, vanadium oxide acts as the catalyst.

96158.q: On which catalyst is ammonia oxidised to nitrogen monoxide in the Ostwald process?
96158.e: The gas mixture flows very quickly through hot gauzes made of platinum and rhodium. Nitric acid is then made from the NO.
96158.m: In the Ostwald process, a platinum-rhodium gauze glows.

96159.q: What did Gerhard Ertl receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 2007?
a: for studies of chemical processes on solid surfaces
96159.e: Among other things, Ertl worked out how nitrogen is split on iron and how CO is oxidised on platinum. In doing so he explained the basics of heterogeneous catalysis.
96159.m: Gerhard Ertl unravelled the chemistry on catalyst surfaces.

96160.q: Why is a solid catalyst on which the particles are bound very strongly unsuitable?
a: The products no longer come off the surface.
The reactants do not reach the surface at all.
The catalyst is used up in the process.
96160.e: If the products stick to the surface, they block the active sites. So a good catalyst binds the particles neither too weakly nor too strongly.
96160.m: A good catalyst binds moderately strongly.

96161.q: Which metal is used as a catalyst for hardening fats to make margarine?
96161.e: Finely divided nickel adds hydrogen to the double bonds of unsaturated vegetable oils. This makes the fats firmer.
96161.m: Nickel helps harden liquid oils into solid fat.

96162.q: Which three researchers received the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing the transistor?
96162.e: William Shockley, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain were honoured in 1956 for their research on semiconductors and the discovery of the transistor effect. Bardeen later received a second Nobel Prize for the theory of superconductivity.
96162.m: Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain shared the 1956 Nobel Prize for the transistor.

96163.q: What are the three terminals of a bipolar transistor called?
96163.e: In a bipolar transistor, a small current into the base controls a larger current between collector and emitter. Gate, source and drain, on the other hand, belong to the field-effect transistor.
96163.m: A bipolar transistor has base, emitter and collector as its terminals.

96164.q: In a MOSFET, what is the terminal called through which the transistor is controlled?
96164.e: In a MOSFET, the gate sits insulated above the channel. A voltage at the gate controls the current flow between source and drain.
96164.m: The current flow in a MOSFET is controlled at the gate.

96165.q: Unlike a bipolar transistor, how is a field-effect transistor controlled?
a: By a voltage at the gate
By a current into the base
By the temperature of the housing
96165.e: The gate of a field-effect transistor is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer, so practically no control current flows at rest. A bipolar transistor, on the other hand, needs a base current.
96165.m: A field-effect transistor is controlled by a voltage, a bipolar transistor by a current.

96166.q: A bipolar transistor has a current gain B of 150. What collector current flows with a base current of 0.2 mA?
96166.e: The collector current is B times the base current: 150 · 0.2 mA makes 30 mA.
96166.m: The collector current is roughly the current gain times the base current.

96167.q: Which two basic types of bipolar transistor are distinguished by the order of their layers?
96167.e: A bipolar transistor consists of three semiconductor layers. Depending on the order of the n and p layers, it is called an NPN or a PNP transistor.
96167.m: Bipolar transistors come as NPN and PNP types.

96168.q: Which technology combines n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs so that almost no current flows at rest?
96168.e: In CMOS circuits, one of the two complementary transistors is switched off in every stable state. Current flows almost only when switching, which is why CMOS is the standard technology for processors today.
96168.m: CMOS circuits use current mainly when they switch.

96169.q: Which two English words make up the name “transistor”?
96169.e: The name was coined at Bell Labs in 1948 as a blend of “transfer” and “resistor”. It describes a resistor that can be controlled by a signal.
96169.m: The word transistor is made up of transfer and resistor.

96170.q: What is the name for connecting two bipolar transistors so that their current gains roughly multiply?
96170.e: In a Darlington pair, the emitter current of the first transistor drives the base of the second. The total gain is about the product of the two individual gains.
96170.m: A Darlington pair reaches a very high current gain using two transistors.

96171.q: From what forward voltage does a silicon diode start to conduct noticeably?
96171.e: For silicon, the threshold voltage of the pn junction is about 0.6 to 0.7 V. Below that, only a very small current flows.
96171.m: A silicon diode only conducts properly from about 0.7 volts.

96172.q: Which diode is deliberately operated in breakdown in the reverse direction to stabilise a voltage?
96172.e: A Zener diode has a precisely set breakdown voltage. In breakdown, the voltage stays almost constant, even when the current varies.
96172.m: A Zener diode can be used to stabilise a voltage.

96173.q: Which junction characterises a Schottky diode?
a: A pn junction made of germanium
Two pn junctions connected back to back
96173.e: In a Schottky diode, a metal contact forms the barrier layer directly with the semiconductor. It has a small forward voltage and switches very quickly.
96173.m: A Schottky diode is based on a junction between metal and semiconductor.

96174.q: How many diodes does a bridge rectifier for single-phase alternating current need?
96174.e: The Graetz bridge consists of four diodes. It redirects both half-waves so that the output always has the same polarity.
96174.m: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes and both half-waves.

96175.q: What is the region at a pn junction called in which there are hardly any free charge carriers?
96175.e: At the boundary between the n and p regions, electrons and holes recombine. What remains is a zone with fixed ions, the depletion region or barrier layer.
96175.m: The depletion region at the pn junction has few free charge carriers.

96176.q: Why is a flyback diode connected in parallel with a relay coil?
a: To get rid of the voltage spike when switching off
To switch the coil on faster
To double the current through the coil
To protect the coil from overheating during operation
96176.e: When switched off, the coil tries to keep the current flowing and produces a high induced voltage. The flyback diode lets this current circulate and so protects the switching transistor.
96176.m: A flyback diode protects switches from a coil's switch-off voltage.

96177.q: According to the Shockley equation, how does the forward current of a diode depend on the applied voltage?
96177.e: The Shockley equation contains an exponential function of the voltage. So even a small increase in voltage makes the current rise sharply.
96177.m: The diode current grows exponentially with the voltage.

96178.q: Which diode produces a current when light falls on it and is used, for example, in light barriers?
96178.e: In a photodiode, photons create electron-hole pairs in the barrier layer. This makes a current flow that depends on the light intensity.
96178.m: A photodiode turns light into an electric current.

96179.q: Which element is often used for p-doping silicon?
96179.e: Boron has three valence electrons. In the silicon lattice one bonding electron is therefore missing, creating a hole as a positive charge carrier.

96180.q: Which charge carriers are in the majority in a p-doped semiconductor?
96180.e: The acceptor atoms create many holes in the p region. They are the majority charge carriers; electrons are in the minority there.
96180.m: In a p-type semiconductor, the current is carried mainly by holes.

96181.q: How many valence electrons does a donor atom that makes silicon n-type have?
96181.e: Donors such as arsenic come from group 15 and have five valence electrons. Four bond with the lattice, and the fifth becomes a free electron.
96181.m: A donor brings one more valence electron than silicon.

96182.q: What do you call foreign atoms that take up an electron in a semiconductor and so create holes?
96182.e: Acceptors have one valence electron fewer than the base material. They capture an electron from the lattice and leave a mobile hole behind.
96182.m: Acceptors take up electrons and create holes.

96183.q: Which process shoots dopant atoms with high energy precisely into a silicon wafer?
96183.e: In ion implantation, foreign atoms are ionised, accelerated electrically and shot into the crystal. Energy and dose determine the depth and concentration of the doping.
96183.m: In ion implantation, dopant atoms are shot into the wafer.

96184.q: What do you call a completely undoped semiconductor that conducts only through intrinsic conduction?
96184.e: In an intrinsic semiconductor, free charge carriers are created only by bonds broken by heat. Electrons and holes occur there in equal numbers.
96184.m: An intrinsic semiconductor is pure and undoped.

96185.q: How many valence electrons does a silicon atom have?
96185.e: Silicon is in group 14 of the periodic table. With its four valence electrons it forms a diamond lattice with four bonds per atom.

96186.q: Why is a wafer heated after ion implantation?
a: To heal crystal damage and activate the dopant atoms
To make the wafer softer for sawing
96186.e: The implanted ions partly destroy the crystal lattice. During annealing the lattice reorganises, and the foreign atoms settle on lattice sites where they have an electrical effect.
96186.m: After implantation the wafer has to be annealed.

96187.q: What is the classic chip package with two parallel rows of pins for through-hole mounting called?
96187.e: DIP stands for “Dual In-line Package”. The pins are pushed through holes in the circuit board, which is why this package is popular for learning circuits on breadboards.
96187.m: A DIP package has two rows of pins for pushing through holes.

96188.q: In which region of the USA did many early chip makers such as Fairchild and Intel appear?
a: In Texas on the Gulf Coast
In New York on the East Coast
96188.e: The area south of San Francisco was named after the semiconductor material silicon. It was there, at Fairchild in 1959, that the Geneva physicist Jean Hoerni invented the planar process.
96188.m: Silicon Valley is named after the chip material silicon.

96189.q: Which semiconductor material was the first integrated circuit of 1958 made of?
96189.e: Kilby's first circuit was built on a small piece of germanium, and the components were still connected with fine gold wires. Silicon only took over afterwards.
96189.m: The first integrated circuit was made of germanium.

96190.q: What do you call a chip that is designed especially for a single application?
96190.e: ASIC stands for “Application-Specific Integrated Circuit”. Such chips are optimised for one task, for example Bitcoin mining or hearing aids.
96190.m: An ASIC is an application-specific chip.

96191.q: What is an integrated circuit called whose logic the user can configure themselves after manufacture?
96191.e: An FPGA (“Field Programmable Gate Array”) contains many programmable logic blocks. How they are connected is only decided when it is used and can be changed.
96191.m: An FPGA can be reprogrammed after manufacture.

96192.q: What do you call a chip that combines the processor, graphics, memory control and other functions of a whole system?
96192.e: A system on a chip (SoC) puts almost all the functions of a computer on a single piece of silicon. Smartphones nearly always use such chips.
96192.m: A system on a chip contains a whole computer system.

96193.q: What is the thin, round silicon disc on which many chips are made at the same time called?
96193.e: Many identical circuits are created side by side on a wafer. Then the disc is sawn up and each piece is built into a package.
96193.m: Chips are made on round silicon discs called wafers.

96194.q: What diameter do the largest silicon wafers used in mass chip production have (as of 2026)?
96194.e: Modern chip factories work with wafers 300 mm in diameter. Plans for 450 mm have not yet been put into mass production.
96194.m: Modern chips are made on wafers 300 millimetres in diameter.

96195.q: What does the abbreviation VLSI stand for?
96195.e: VLSI means integrating a very large number of transistors on a single chip. The exact boundaries between LSI, VLSI and ULSI are given differently in the technical literature.
96195.m: VLSI means integration on a very large scale.

96196.q: In which year did Gordon Moore publish the article on which Moore's law is based?
96196.e: In 1965 Moore wrote in the journal “Electronics” about the growing number of components per chip. This later became Moore's law.
96196.m: Moore's law goes back to an article from 1965.

96197.q: Which company did Gordon Moore found together with Robert Noyce in 1968?
96197.e: Moore and Noyce left Fairchild Semiconductor and founded Intel in 1968. Moore later led the company for a long time.
96197.m: Gordon Moore was a co-founder of Intel.

96198.q: What doubling period did Moore give in his original forecast of 1965?
96198.e: In 1965 Moore predicted that the number of components per chip would double every year. In 1975 he adjusted the forecast to a longer period.
96198.m: In 1965 Moore first expected doubling every year.

96199.q: A chip has 1 billion transistors. How many would a chip have after 10 years if the number doubles every 2 years?
96199.e: In 10 years there are 5 doublings. 2 to the power of 5 is 32, so 32 billion transistors.
96199.m: Exponential growth doubles a quantity at equal intervals of time.

96200.q: What kind of statement is Moore's law?
a: A natural law of quantum physics
96200.e: Moore's law describes an observed trend in the semiconductor industry. It is not a law of nature and only holds as long as technology and the economy allow it.
96200.m: Moore's law is an observation, not a law of nature.

96201.q: Why can Moore's law not continue for ever?
a: Because transistors cannot become smaller than a few atoms
Because there is no more silicon on Earth
Because computers are not allowed to get faster
96201.e: The smallest structures on chips today measure only a few nanometres, that is a few dozen atoms. With even smaller structures, quantum effects such as leakage currents cause problems. On top of that, cooling becomes harder and harder.
96201.m: Physical limits are slowing down Moore's law.

96202.q: Why did processor clock speeds hardly rise any more from about 2005?
a: Because software cannot use higher clock speeds
Because standards limit the clock speed
96202.e: Higher clock speeds would have produced so much waste heat that the chips could no longer have been cooled. The manufacturers therefore turned to several processor cores per chip.
96202.m: Heat limits the clock speed of modern processors.

96203.q: How do the costs of new chip factories develop as the structures become smaller and smaller?
96203.e: Ever finer structures require more expensive machines and cleaner rooms. A modern chip factory today costs over ten billion dollars. The rule of thumb for this is called Rock's law.
96203.m: New chip factories are getting more and more expensive.

96204.q: What is the light-sensitive layer called that is applied to the wafer in photolithography?
96204.e: The photoresist changes its solubility when exposed to light. In this way a pattern can be transferred onto it, which then serves as a stencil for etching or doping.
96204.m: Photoresist transfers the pattern of the mask onto the wafer.

96205.q: What do you call the template with the pattern that is projected onto the wafer in photolithography?
96205.e: The photomask is usually a quartz glass plate with chrome structures. Its pattern is normally projected onto the wafer at a reduced size.
96205.m: A photomask contains the pattern of one chip layer.

96206.q: Which company is the only manufacturer of EUV lithography machines for mass chip production (as of 2026)?
96206.e: The Dutch company ASML is the only one supplying EUV machines for mass production. Its customers include TSMC, Samsung and Intel.
96206.m: All EUV lithography machines for mass production come from ASML.

96207.q: Why are chips exposed with shorter and shorter wavelengths?
a: So that finer structures can be produced
So that the chips use less electricity
So that the photoresist dries faster
So that the wafers get bigger
96207.e: Light cannot reproduce structures much smaller than its wavelength. That is why the industry moved from visible light to deep ultraviolet and then to extreme ultraviolet.
96207.m: The shorter the wavelength, the finer the chip structures that can be exposed.

96208.q: Why are computer chips made in a clean room?
a: Even tiny dust particles can destroy the fine structures
Because the light is brighter there
Because the machines would otherwise be too loud
96208.e: The structures on chips are much smaller than a speck of dust. In clean rooms the air is heavily filtered and the staff wear protective suits.
96208.m: Chips are made in dust-free clean rooms.

96209.q: What kind of light is used today to expose the finest structures of computer chips?
96209.e: Photolithography uses deep and extreme ultraviolet. This light has a much shorter wavelength than visible light and therefore allows finer structures.
96209.m: Chips are exposed with ultraviolet light.

96210.q: Why do EUV lithography machines use mirrors instead of lenses?
a: Because almost all materials strongly absorb EUV light
Because mirrors are cheaper than lenses
Because lenses focus the light too strongly
Because EUV light is not refracted but bends
96210.e: Extreme ultraviolet is swallowed even by glass and air. That is why EUV machines work in a vacuum with specially coated mirrors.
96210.m: EUV light is guided with mirrors in a vacuum.

96211.q: With a positive resist, what happens to the exposed areas during developing?
96211.e: With a positive resist, the light makes the resist soluble and the developer removes the exposed areas. With a negative resist it is the other way round.
96211.m: With a positive resist, the exposed areas disappear.

96212.q: What do you call a lithography machine that exposes the wafer field by field, one after another?
96212.e: The stepper moves the wafer step by step under the lens and exposes each field separately. Modern scanners also move the mask and wafer in sync while doing so.
96212.m: A stepper exposes a wafer step by step.

96213.q: What voltage gain does an inverting amplifier have with R1 equal to 10 kΩ and a feedback resistor R2 equal to 47 kΩ?
96213.e: For an inverting amplifier, v equals -R2 / R1. So -47 kΩ / 10 kΩ gives -4.7.
96213.m: An inverting amplifier reverses the sign of the signal.

96214.q: What voltage gain does a non-inverting amplifier have with R1 equal to 1 kΩ (to ground) and R2 equal to 9 kΩ (feedback)?
96214.e: For a non-inverting amplifier, v equals 1 + R2 / R1. So 1 + 9 kΩ / 1 kΩ gives 10.
96214.m: A non-inverting amplifier always amplifies by at least a factor of one.

96215.q: What input resistance does an ideal operational amplifier have?
96215.e: An ideal operational amplifier draws no current at its inputs. This corresponds to an infinitely large input resistance.
96215.m: An ideal operational amplifier does not load the signal source.

96216.q: What voltage appears between the two inputs of an operational amplifier with ideal negative feedback?
96216.e: The negative feedback adjusts the output until the difference between the inputs disappears. This is called a virtual ground or a virtual short circuit.
96216.m: With negative feedback, both inputs of an ideal operational amplifier have the same voltage.

96217.q: What voltage gain does a voltage follower (buffer) have?
96217.e: In a voltage follower, the output is connected directly to the inverting input. The output voltage follows the input voltage exactly but can supply much more current.
96217.m: A voltage follower passes the signal on unchanged but able to drive a load.

96218.q: What do you call an operational amplifier without negative feedback that only shows which of two voltages is larger?
96218.e: Without negative feedback, the huge open-loop gain takes full effect. So the output jumps to the upper or lower limit even with tiny differences.
96218.m: A comparator compares two voltages with each other.

96219.q: What is an operational amplifier such as the well-known µA741?
a: An integrated circuit that strongly amplifies voltage differences
96219.e: An operational amplifier is a small chip with two inputs and one output. It strongly amplifies the difference between the input voltages. The µA741 from 1968 became a classic in schools and devices.
96219.m: An operational amplifier amplifies voltage differences.

96220.q: Where does the operational amplifier get its name from?
a: It carried out mathematical operations in analogue computers
It was first used in operating theatres
It only works during one operation of the processor
It was invented by a military operations team
96220.e: With the right circuit, the amplifier can add, subtract, integrate and differentiate. That is exactly what it was built for in analogue computers.
96220.m: Operational amplifiers got their name because they carried out mathematical operations.

96221.q: In an integrator, which component sits in the feedback path of the operational amplifier?
96221.e: The capacitor collects the input current. Its voltage, and therefore the output voltage, corresponds to the integral of the input signal.
96221.m: In an integrator, there is a capacitor in the feedback path.

96222.q: In which unit is the capacitance of a capacitor measured?
96222.e: One farad is the capacitance at which 1 coulomb of charge produces a voltage of 1 volt. The unit is named after Michael Faraday.

96223.q: How does the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor change if you double the distance between the plates?
96223.e: For a parallel-plate capacitor, C equals ε times A divided by d. The distance d is in the denominator, so double the distance gives half the capacitance.
96223.m: The larger the distance between the plates, the smaller the capacitance.

96224.q: How much energy does a 100 µF capacitor store at a voltage of 10 V?
96224.e: W equals ½ · C · U². So 0.5 · 0.0001 F · 100 V² gives 0.005 J, that is 5 mJ.
96224.m: The energy in a capacitor grows with the square of the voltage.

96225.q: What is the time constant of an RC circuit with 10 kΩ and 100 µF?
96225.e: The time constant is τ equals R · C. 10,000 Ω · 0.0001 F gives 1 second.
96225.m: The time constant of an RC circuit is resistance multiplied by capacitance.

96226.q: After how many time constants is a capacitor charging through a resistor considered practically full?
96226.e: After one time constant, the capacitor is about 63 per cent charged, after five more than 99 per cent. That is why it is then considered practically full.
96226.m: After five time constants a capacitor is almost completely charged.

96227.q: What is the total capacitance of two capacitors of 10 µF each connected in series?
96227.e: In series, the reciprocals add up: 1/10 + 1/10 gives 1/5. So the total capacitance is 5 µF.
96227.m: Capacitors in series together have less capacitance than each one alone.

96228.q: Which type of capacitor is polarised and can be destroyed if connected the wrong way round?
96228.e: In an electrolytic capacitor, the dielectric forms as a thin oxide layer on the anode. With the wrong polarity this layer breaks down, and the capacitor can heat up and burst.
96228.m: An electrolytic capacitor must be connected with the correct polarity.

96229.q: How does the reactance of a capacitor change when the frequency rises?
96229.e: Capacitive reactance is X equals 1 / (2πfC). So high frequencies pass through a capacitor more easily than low ones.
96229.m: A capacitor lets high frequencies through better than low ones.

96230.q: Which quantity does an oscilloscope show on the vertical axis by default?
96230.e: An oscilloscope shows how a voltage changes over time. Time is on the horizontal axis and voltage on the vertical axis.
96230.m: An oscilloscope shows voltage over time.

96231.q: Which function on an oscilloscope makes a periodic signal appear as a stationary picture?
96231.e: The trigger starts every recording at the same point of the signal, for example on a rising edge. As a result, the curves lie exactly on top of each other.
96231.m: The trigger keeps the picture on the oscilloscope steady.

96232.q: One period of a signal is 4 divisions wide, and the time base is set to 5 ms per division. What is the frequency of the signal?
96232.e: The period is 4 · 5 ms equals 20 ms. The frequency is 1 / 0.02 s equals 50 Hz.
96232.m: The frequency is the reciprocal of the period.

96233.q: A sine wave is 6 divisions high from peak to peak, with 2 V per division set. What is the amplitude?
96233.e: From peak to peak it is 6 · 2 V equals 12 V. The amplitude is half of that, so 6 V.
96233.m: The amplitude is half the peak-to-peak voltage.

96234.q: By what factor does a standard 10:1 probe reduce the measured signal?
96234.e: The probe divides the voltage in the ratio 10 to 1. In return it loads the circuit less, and the oscilloscope usually scales the display back automatically.
96234.m: A 10:1 probe divides the signal by ten.

96235.q: Which tube was the heart of classic analogue oscilloscopes?
96235.e: In the Braun tube, voltages deflect an electron beam that draws a trace on the fluorescent screen. Ferdinand Braun developed it in 1897.
96235.m: Analogue oscilloscopes drew on the screen with an electron beam.

96236.q: Which figures appear in XY mode when two sine signals are plotted against each other?
96236.e: In XY mode, one signal controls the horizontal deflection and the other the vertical. Depending on the frequency ratio and phase, ellipses, figures of eight and other Lissajous figures appear.
96236.m: Two sine signals in XY mode produce Lissajous figures.

96237.q: What does the bandwidth of an oscilloscope indicate?
a: The frequency at which a sine wave is shown reduced by 3 dB
The largest voltage that can be displayed
The width of the screen in divisions
96237.e: At the bandwidth limit, a sine signal is shown with only about 71 per cent of its amplitude. For accurate measurements, the bandwidth should be well above the signal frequency.
96237.m: The bandwidth limits how fast the signals are that an oscilloscope shows correctly.

96238.q: Which semiconductor component can be switched on with a trigger pulse but not switched off again via the control terminal?
96238.e: Once triggered, a thyristor stays conducting until the current falls below the holding current. This makes it especially suitable for very high currents in alternating current applications.
96238.m: A triggered thyristor conducts until the current is almost zero.

96239.q: Which component combines the simple control of a MOSFET with the high current capacity of a bipolar transistor?
96239.e: IGBT means “Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor”. It is controlled through an insulated gate and can switch large currents at high voltages, for example in locomotives.
96239.m: The IGBT is a voltage-controlled power switch for high currents.

96240.q: Which semiconductor materials with a wide band gap are increasingly being used in modern power electronics?
96240.e: Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) can handle higher voltages, temperatures and switching frequencies than silicon. They make chargers smaller and electric cars more efficient, for example.
96240.m: Silicon carbide and gallium nitride make more efficient power electronics possible.

96241.q: What is the method called in which an average voltage is set by switching on and off quickly with a variable on-time?
96241.e: In pulse-width modulation (PWM), the switching frequency stays the same; only the ratio of on-time to off-time changes. This gives the desired average value.
96241.m: Pulse-width modulation sets average values by fast switching.

96242.q: What is a DC-DC converter called that turns a higher DC voltage into a lower one?
96242.e: The buck converter (step-down converter) switches the input voltage onto a coil in pulses. With a diode and a capacitor, a smoothed lower voltage is produced.
96242.m: A buck converter turns a high DC voltage into a lower one.

96243.q: An ideal buck converter is supplied with 48 V and is switched on 25 per cent of the time. What output voltage does it deliver?
96243.e: In an ideal buck converter, the output voltage is the on-time fraction times the input voltage. 0.25 · 48 V gives 12 V.
96243.m: In a buck converter, the on-time fraction determines the output voltage.

96244.q: Why do switched-mode power supplies work with much lower losses than linear regulators?
a: Because the transistors are only ever fully on or fully off
Because they only work with alternating current
96244.e: A fully switched-on transistor has hardly any voltage drop, and a switched-off one carries hardly any current. In both cases little power is lost, whereas a linear regulator burns off the excess voltage as heat.
96244.m: Switching instead of regulating saves energy in power electronics.

96245.q: Which device controls the speed of a three-phase motor by changing frequency and voltage?
96245.e: A frequency converter first rectifies the mains voltage and uses it to produce three-phase current with adjustable frequency. This way pumps, fans and trains run exactly as fast as needed.
96245.m: A frequency converter lets you adjust a motor's speed smoothly.

96246.q: Which function of a solar inverter constantly searches for the operating point at which the panels deliver the most power?
96246.e: MPP stands for “Maximum Power Point”. Because this point shifts with light and temperature, the inverter constantly adjusts voltage and current.
96246.m: MPP tracking gets the maximum out of the solar panels.

96247.q: What must a grid-connected inverter match with the power grid before feeding in electricity?
96247.e: The inverter must feed in exactly in step with the grid. If the frequency or phase were wrong, large balancing currents would flow.
96247.m: An inverter must synchronise exactly with the grid.

96248.q: What efficiency do modern solar inverters typically reach?
96248.e: Modern devices lose only a few per cent of the energy as heat. Exactly 100 per cent is physically impossible.
96248.m: Good inverters convert solar power with hardly any losses.

96249.q: What do you call an inverter that forms its own power network without the public grid, for example on a remote mountain hut?
96249.e: An off-grid inverter itself produces a stable alternating voltage with a fixed frequency, usually from a battery. It is used where there is no grid connection.
96249.m: An off-grid inverter supplies a network not connected to the public power grid.

96250.q: What must a grid-connected inverter do if the public power grid fails?
a: Keep feeding in at full power
Reconnect the solar panels in series
96250.e: A grid and system protection device disconnects the inverter within a short time if the grid fails. This stops a switched-off grid from suddenly becoming live, which would endanger engineers working on it.
96250.m: If the grid fails, a grid-connected inverter must switch off immediately.

96251.q: What is a small inverter mounted directly on a single solar panel called?
96251.e: A module inverter (microinverter) converts the current of each panel separately. As a result, a shaded panel does not slow down the others.
96251.m: A module inverter works separately for each solar panel.

96252.q: Why does an electric car with a three-phase motor need an inverter?
a: To produce three-phase current for the motor from the battery's DC voltage
To charge the battery from a household socket
To supply the radio with electricity
To keep the battery voltage constant
96252.e: The battery supplies DC voltage, but the motor needs three-phase alternating current with a variable frequency. The drive inverter produces it and so controls speed and torque.
96252.m: In an electric car, the inverter turns battery current into three-phase current.

96253.q: Which circuit of four switches forms the basic design of a single-phase inverter?
96253.e: In an H-bridge, two diagonally opposite switches switch at the same time. By switching back and forth, the current flows through the load first in one direction, then in the other.
96253.m: An H-bridge can reverse the direction of current through a load.

96254.q: What are clean rooms divided into clean room classes by?
a: By the permitted number of particles in the air
By the size of the room
By the number of people in the room
96254.e: The international standard ISO 14644-1 sets the maximum number of particles of a certain size allowed in one cubic metre of air.
96254.m: Clean room classes depend on the number of particles in the air.

96255.q: Which ISO clean room class is the cleanest?
96255.e: The smaller the class number, the fewer particles are allowed. ISO 1 is the strictest class; ISO 9 roughly corresponds to normal room air.
96255.m: With clean rooms, a smaller class number means greater cleanliness.

96256.q: What is the even, low-turbulence airflow from the ceiling to the floor in many clean rooms called?
96256.e: In laminar flow, the air moves in parallel layers. Particles are thus carried straight down instead of swirling around the room.
96256.m: Laminar airflow carries particles evenly away in a clean room.

96257.q: Which filters are particularly effective at holding back airborne particles in clean rooms?
96257.e: HEPA and ULPA filters remove even very small particles almost completely. They are usually in the ceiling above the work area.
96257.m: HEPA and ULPA filters clean the air in a clean room.

96258.q: Why is there usually a slight overpressure in clean rooms compared with their surroundings?
a: So that no unfiltered air gets in
So that the machines are cooled better
So that people can breathe more easily
So that doors close by themselves
96258.e: With overpressure, air always flows outwards through gaps and open doors. Unfiltered, dusty outside air therefore does not get into the clean room.
96258.m: Overpressure keeps dirt out of a clean room.

96259.q: What is usually the biggest source of particles in a clean room?
96259.e: People constantly shed skin flakes, hair and fibres. That is why everyone in a clean room wears overalls, a hood, a face mask and gloves.
96259.m: In a clean room, people are the biggest source of dirt.

96260.q: Why is the light yellow in the lithography areas of chip factories?
a: Because the photoresist reacts to short-wavelength light
Because yellow light makes dust visible
96260.e: Photoresist is sensitive to blue and ultraviolet light. Yellow light does not contain these short wavelengths and so does not expose the resist by accident.
96260.m: Yellow light protects the photoresist from unwanted exposure.

96261.q: Which research centre in Rüschlikon, opened in 2011 with a large clean room for nanotechnology, is run jointly by IBM and ETH Zurich?
96261.e: The centre is on the site of IBM Research Zurich in Rüschlikon. It is named after the Nobel Prize winners Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer.
96261.m: In Rüschlikon, IBM and ETH do research together in a nanotechnology clean room.

96262.q: How many layers does the OSI reference model have?
96262.e: The OSI model divides network communication into seven layers, from the physical layer up to the application layer. The more practical TCP/IP model manages with fewer layers.
96262.m: The OSI model has seven layers.

96263.q: On which OSI layer does a router mainly work?
96263.e: A router forwards packets between different networks based on their logical destination address. Choosing this route is the job of the network layer.
96263.m: Routers work on the network layer of the OSI model.

96264.q: Which OSI layer provides the end-to-end connection between programs, for example with TCP?
96264.e: The transport layer (layer 4) connects processes on two computers. Depending on the protocol, it takes care of ordering, flow control and retransmission.
96264.m: The transport layer connects applications end to end.

96265.q: Which OSI layer describes cables, plugs, radio signals and the transmission of individual bits?
96265.e: Layer 1 defines how bits are physically transmitted as voltage, light or radio waves. Plugs and cable types belong to it too.
96265.m: The lowest OSI layer transmits raw bits.

96266.q: What is it called when data is given an extra header at each layer on its way down?
96266.e: Each layer wraps the data of the layer above and adds its own control information. At the receiver, the wrappers are removed again in reverse order.
96266.m: With encapsulation, each layer gets its own header.

96267.q: Which organisation published the OSI reference model as a standard?
96267.e: OSI stands for “Open Systems Interconnection”. The model was published as standard ISO 7498 by the International Organization for Standardization, based in Geneva.
96267.m: The OSI model is an ISO standard.

96268.q: What is the data unit on the data link layer (layer 2) called?
96268.e: On layer 2, data is packed into frames containing the destination and source address and a checksum. On layer 3 you speak of packets, on layer 4 with TCP of segments.
96268.m: On the data link layer, the data units are called frames.

96269.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for data formats, character encoding and partly for encryption?
96269.e: The presentation layer (layer 6) makes sure that sender and receiver understand the data in the same format. This includes things such as character sets and compression.
96269.m: The presentation layer translates data formats between systems.

96270.q: How many root server addresses named with letters are there in the DNS?
96270.e: The root servers are called a.root-servers.net to m.root-servers.net. Thanks to anycast, more than a thousand individual servers worldwide stand behind the 13 names.
96270.m: The DNS has thirteen named root server addresses.

96271.q: Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv6 address?
96271.e: The A record contains an IPv4 address. Because IPv6 addresses are four times as long, the corresponding record is called AAAA.
96271.m: An AAAA record points to an IPv6 address.

96272.q: Which DNS record states which server receives the emails for a domain?
96272.e: MX stands for “Mail Exchange”. A sending mail server looks up this record to know where to send a message.
96272.m: The MX record points to the mail server of a domain.

96273.q: Which DNS record type makes one name an alias for another name?
96273.e: CNAME means “Canonical Name”. This lets www.example.ch, for example, point to another host name whose address is then resolved.
96273.m: A CNAME record is an alias for another name.

96274.q: Which foundation runs the registry of the Swiss top-level domain .ch?
96274.e: SWITCH has managed the database of all .ch domains for decades and runs the name servers for it. You can register .ch domains with many registrars.
96274.m: SWITCH runs the registry of the .ch domain.

96275.q: What do you call a DNS server that resolves a query for a client step by step with other name servers?
96275.e: The recursive resolver queries root, top-level and authoritative servers one after another. It caches the result so that later queries are faster.
96275.m: A recursive resolver does the whole name resolution for the client.

96276.q: Which extension protects DNS answers against forgery with digital signatures?
96276.e: DNSSEC signs the DNS data cryptographically. A resolver can thus check whether an answer is genuine and does not come from an attacker.
96276.m: DNSSEC protects DNS answers against forgery.

96277.q: Who designed the Domain Name System in 1983?
96277.e: Paul Mockapetris described the DNS in 1983 in RFCs 882 and 883. Before that, all computer names were kept in a single file called HOSTS.TXT.
96277.m: Paul Mockapetris is the inventor of the DNS.

96278.q: Which DNS record type is used for reverse lookup from an IP address to a name?
96278.e: PTR stands for “Pointer”. Such records live in special zones such as in-addr.arpa and point from an address to a host name.
96278.m: A PTR record resolves an IP address into a name.

96279.q: What does the HTTP status code 404 mean?
a: The requested resource was not found
96279.e: 404 means “Not Found”: the server can be reached but does not know the requested address. Forbidden access would have the code 403.
96279.m: Status code 404 means that a page was not found.

96280.q: Which class of HTTP status codes indicates an error on the server?
96280.e: Codes from 500 upwards report server errors such as 500 “Internal Server Error”. The 4xx codes, on the other hand, stand for errors caused by the client.
96280.m: HTTP status codes starting with 5 report server errors.

96281.q: Which HTTP method do you typically use to send form data to the server in the body of the request?
96281.e: With POST, the data is in the body of the request, not in the URL. GET, by contrast, is mainly used to fetch resources.
96281.m: You use POST to send data to a web server.

96282.q: HTTP is stateless. How do websites still remember a login, for example, across several requests?
96282.e: The server sends a small piece of data that the browser sends back with every further request. It usually contains a session ID.
96282.m: Cookies give stateless HTTP a memory.

96283.q: At which research centre did Tim Berners-Lee develop HTTP from 1989?
96283.e: In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee proposed a linked information system at CERN near Geneva. This led to HTTP, HTML and the World Wide Web.
96283.m: The World Wide Web with HTTP was created at CERN.

96285.q: Which HTTP status code indicates a permanent redirect?
96285.e: 301 means “Moved Permanently”. Browsers and search engines remember the new address, whereas 302 is only a temporary redirect.
96285.m: Status code 301 announces that a page has moved permanently.

96286.q: What new feature did HTTP/2 bring compared with HTTP/1.1?
a: Several requests in parallel over one connection
96286.e: HTTP/2 splits requests into binary frames and sends several data streams at once over a single connection. This multiplexing makes web pages faster.
96286.m: HTTP/2 transmits several requests at once over one connection.

96287.q: What was the predecessor protocol of TLS developed by Netscape called?
96287.e: Secure Sockets Layer was introduced by Netscape in the mid-1990s. TLS 1.0 followed in 1999 as a further development; today all SSL versions are considered insecure.
96287.m: TLS is the successor of SSL.

96288.q: How can you tell in the browser that a website is encrypted with TLS?
96288.e: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. Browsers often also show a padlock symbol. The current version is TLS 1.3 from 2018.
96288.m: TLS 1.3 is the most modern version of the protocol.

96289.q: How is the actual payload encrypted in TLS after the handshake?
a: Symmetrically with a shared session key
Asymmetrically with the server's public key
Not at all, only the login is encrypted
96289.e: Asymmetric methods are only used to agree on the key and for authentication. For the large amount of data, TLS uses fast symmetric methods such as AES.
96289.m: TLS encrypts the data symmetrically once the key has been agreed.

96290.q: Which property prevents a server key stolen later from decrypting old, recorded TLS sessions?
96290.e: With Perfect Forward Secrecy, a short-lived key is agreed for each session and then discarded. TLS 1.3 always relies on such short-lived keys for key exchange.
96290.m: Forward secrecy protects past sessions even if a key is lost later.

96291.q: What was the serious security flaw discovered in 2014 in the widely used TLS library OpenSSL called?
96291.e: A bug in the heartbeat extension made it possible to read parts of the server's memory, including private keys. Millions of servers had to be updated.
96291.m: Heartbleed was a serious flaw in OpenSSL.

96292.q: What does the browser check using the server certificate when setting up a TLS connection?
a: Whether the server really belongs to the domain requested
Whether the server is fast enough
Whether the server is in Switzerland
96292.e: The certificate confirms that the public key belongs to the domain. If something is wrong, the browser shows a warning.
96292.m: The certificate proves that you are talking to the right server.

96293.q: Which non-profit certificate authority has issued free, automatically renewable TLS certificates since 2015?
96293.e: Let's Encrypt automates issuing through the ACME protocol. As a result, the share of encrypted websites rose sharply.
96293.m: Let's Encrypt made TLS certificates free and automatic.

96294.q: Between which levels is TLS located in the network stack?
a: Between the transport and the application protocol
Between the cable and the network card
Inside the operating system kernel below IP
96294.e: TLS runs on a reliable transport connection such as TCP. Application protocols such as HTTP, SMTP or IMAP then run encrypted on top of it.
96294.m: TLS sits between the transport connection and the application.

96295.q: Which protocol exchanges routes between the autonomous systems of the internet?
96295.e: The Border Gateway Protocol connects the networks of providers, companies and universities. It chooses routes based on path information and policies.
96295.m: BGP holds the networks of the internet together.

96296.q: How is the default route written in IPv4?
96296.e: The prefix 0.0.0.0/0 matches every destination address. Packets without a more specific route therefore go to the default gateway entered there.
96296.m: The default route 0.0.0.0/0 matches all destinations.

96297.q: A router knows the routes 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16. Which route does it choose for a packet to 10.1.2.3?
96297.e: Both prefixes match, but the router chooses according to the longest prefix match rule. /16 is more specific than /8.
96297.m: A router always chooses the most specific matching route.

96298.q: Which metric does the simple routing protocol RIP use to compare routes?
a: The number of routers on the way
The length of the cables in metres
96298.e: RIP counts the hops, that is the routers up to the destination. From 16 hops a destination counts as unreachable, so RIP is only suitable for small networks.
96298.m: With RIP, a distance of sixteen hops means unreachable.

96299.q: Which tool shows the routers on a packet's way to its destination?
96299.e: Traceroute sends packets with a lifetime that increases step by step. Each router where a packet expires reports back and so reveals its address.
96299.m: With traceroute you can see a packet's path through the network.

96300.q: What is the method called with which a home router hides many private addresses behind a single public IPv4 address?
96300.e: For outgoing packets, the router replaces the private source address with its public one and notes the mapping in a table. This lets it send replies back to the right device.
96300.m: With address translation, many devices share one public IPv4 address.

96301.q: What do you call routing in which an administrator enters the routes by hand?
96301.e: Static routes do not change by themselves when a line fails. They are simple but are mainly suitable for small, clearly structured networks.
96301.m: Static routes are set by hand.

96302.q: What is the advantage of dynamic routing over static routing?
a: Routers adjust their routes themselves when something fails
No routers are needed any more
It only works without the internet
The routes have to be entered by hand every day
96302.e: With dynamic routing, routers constantly exchange information, for example with RIP or OSPF. If a line fails, they automatically find another route.
96302.m: Dynamic routing reacts to failures by itself.

96303.q: What is the counterpart to packet switching called, in which a fixed channel is reserved for the whole connection?
96303.e: The classic telephone network reserved a continuous line for every call. With packet switching, by contrast, many connections share the same lines.
96303.m: Circuit switching reserves a fixed channel for the whole connection.

96304.q: Why is data on the internet split into small packets instead of being sent in one piece?
a: So that many connections can share the same lines
So that the data is automatically encrypted
So that no addresses are needed
So that the lines use less electricity
96304.e: Packets from many users are sent in turn over the same lines. If a packet is lost, only that one has to be sent again. The term “packet” was coined by the Briton Donald Davies.
96304.m: Packet switching uses lines together and efficiently.

96305.q: Which network, launched in 1969, is seen as the forerunner of the internet and used packet switching?
96305.e: From 1969, the ARPANET first connected four university computers in the USA. The internet developed from it and the TCP/IP protocols.
96305.m: The ARPANET was the first large packet-switched network.

96306.q: What can happen because the packets of a message can take different routes through the network?
a: They arrive in a different order
They are decrypted on the way
96306.e: Each packet is forwarded individually and can take a faster or slower route. The receiver therefore has to put the data back in order using sequence numbers.
96306.m: Packets can arrive in the wrong order and have to be sorted.

96307.q: What do you call the principle in which a network node receives a packet completely before forwarding it?
96307.e: With store-and-forward, the whole packet is buffered and checked before it moves on. This costs a little time but prevents faulty packets from being forwarded.
96307.m: With store-and-forward, each packet is received in full and then forwarded.

96308.q: What is the usual maximum payload (MTU) of an Ethernet frame?
96308.e: Standard Ethernet carries at most 1500 bytes of payload per frame. Larger IP packets therefore have to be split up or chosen smaller.
96308.m: A normal Ethernet frame carries at most 1500 bytes of payload.

96309.q: How long does it take to send a 1500-byte packet over a line with 12 Mbit/s?
96309.e: 1500 bytes are 12,000 bits. 12,000 bits divided by 12,000,000 bits/s gives 0.001 s, that is 1 ms.
96309.m: The sending time is the packet size divided by the data rate.

96310.q: In IPv4, what happens to a packet that is larger than the MTU of the next line if the “don't fragment” flag is not set?
a: It is sent back to the sender
It is diverted to another line
96310.e: An IPv4 router may break packets that are too large into smaller fragments. Only the receiver puts them back together.
96310.m: IPv4 packets that are too large can be fragmented on the way.

96311.q: How many bits does a MAC address have in Ethernet and Wi-Fi?
96311.e: A MAC address consists of 6 bytes, that is 48 bits. It is usually written as six hexadecimal pairs, such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.
96311.m: An Ethernet MAC address is 48 bits long.

96312.q: What does the first part of a MAC address, the OUI, indicate?
a: The manufacturer of the network interface
96312.e: The first three bytes form the “Organizationally Unique Identifier”, which the IEEE assigns to manufacturers. The manufacturer numbers the rest itself.
96312.m: From the start of a MAC address you can tell the manufacturer.

96313.q: Which MAC address means “to all devices in the local network”?
96313.e: In the broadcast address, all 48 bits are set to 1. Frames to this address are processed by all devices in the segment.
96313.m: The MAC address made of all Fs is aimed at all devices.

96314.q: Which protocol finds the MAC address for an IP address in a local IPv4 network?
96314.e: With the Address Resolution Protocol, a device asks by broadcast who has a particular IP address. The device being looked for answers with its MAC address.
96314.m: ARP finds the matching MAC address for an IP address.

96315.q: Why do modern smartphones often use random MAC addresses in Wi-Fi networks?
a: So that the device cannot be tracked from place to place
So that the Wi-Fi gets faster
So that the battery lasts longer
So that no IP address is needed
96315.e: A device broadcasts a fixed MAC address everywhere it searches for Wi-Fi networks. With random addresses, shops or railway stations, for example, find it harder to recognise visitors.
96315.m: Random MAC addresses protect privacy on Wi-Fi.

96316.q: How does a switch decide which port to forward a frame to?
a: Using the destination MAC address in its address table
Using the destination IP address in its routing table
It always sends every frame to all ports
96316.e: A switch learns from the source addresses which device is connected to which port. If it does not yet know a destination address, it floods the frame to all ports.
96316.m: A switch forwards frames using learned MAC addresses.

96317.q: What happens to the MAC addresses in a packet when it passes a router?
a: They are set anew for the next section
They stay unchanged all the way to the destination
They are converted into IP addresses
96317.e: MAC addresses are only valid in the local network concerned. The router puts the packet into a new frame with its own and the next MAC address; the IP addresses stay the same.
96317.m: MAC addresses are only valid as far as the next router.

96318.q: What does “MAC” stand for in MAC address?
96318.e: The MAC sublayer controls how several devices access the shared transmission medium. That is also where the hardware address is used.
96318.m: MAC stands for Media Access Control.

96319.q: How many bits does an IPv6 address have?
96319.e: IPv6 addresses are four times as long as IPv4 addresses. This makes a practically unlimited number of addresses available.
96319.m: An IPv6 address is 128 bits long.

96320.q: How often may the abbreviation “::” appear in an IPv6 address?
96320.e: The “::” replaces a sequence of zero blocks. If it appeared more than once, you would no longer know how many zero blocks are missing in which place.
96320.m: The double colon may appear only once in an IPv6 address.

96321.q: What is the correctly shortened form of the IPv6 address 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
96321.e: Leading zeros in each block may be left out, and the long sequence of zero blocks is replaced by “::”. Zeros at the end of a block, as in 2001, stay.
96321.m: In IPv6 you shorten leading zeros and one sequence of zero blocks.

96322.q: What is the loopback address in IPv6?
96322.e: The address ::1 refers to your own device. It consists of 127 zero bits and a 1 at the end.
96322.m: In IPv6 you reach your own device via ::1.

96323.q: What does an IPv6 device receive from the router so that it can create a global address for itself?
96323.e: The router announces which prefix applies in the network. The device forms the rear part of the address itself, without any central server.
96323.m: IPv6 devices form their address from the router's network prefix.

96324.q: Which type of address no longer exists in IPv6, unlike in IPv4?
96324.e: IPv6 does without broadcast and uses targeted multicast instead. That way, not all devices in the network are disturbed unnecessarily.

96325.q: How are the blocks of an IPv6 address written?
96325.e: An IPv6 address consists of eight blocks of four hexadecimal digits each, separated by colons. IPv4, by contrast, is written in decimal with dots.
96325.m: IPv6 addresses are hexadecimal and separated by colons.

96326.q: Why do you usually no longer need address translation (NAT) in a home network with IPv6?
a: There are enough public addresses for every device
IPv6 only works in the local network
96326.e: With IPv4, many devices share one public address, which is why NAT is needed. With 128 bits, IPv6 has so many addresses that every device can get its own.
96326.m: IPv6 offers enough addresses to make NAT unnecessary.

96327.q: How many hexadecimal digits does a fully written-out IPv6 address have?
96327.e: An IPv6 address consists of 8 blocks of 4 hexadecimal digits each. 8 × 4 gives 32 digits.
96327.m: A written-out IPv6 address has thirty-two hexadecimal digits.

96328.q: What is the main aim of a Content Delivery Network?
a: To deliver content from servers close to the users
To translate web pages into other languages
96328.e: A CDN stores copies of images, videos and scripts on many servers worldwide. Short distances mean less delay and less load on the main server.
96328.m: A CDN brings content closer to the users.

96329.q: What are the locations of a CDN called, where servers stand close to the users?
96329.e: At a Point of Presence there are edge servers that cache content. Large CDNs have hundreds of such locations, including in Switzerland.
96329.m: The servers of a CDN stand at Points of Presence.

96330.q: Which company, founded in 1998 out of MIT, is seen as one of the first large CDN providers?
96330.e: Akamai was founded by Tom Leighton and Daniel Lewin. Their algorithms distributed content so that servers would not collapse under heavy demand.
96330.m: Akamai was one of the first large CDN providers.

96331.q: With which addressing method do many CDN servers worldwide share the same IP address?
96331.e: With anycast, the same address is announced in many places. Routing automatically takes each request to the nearest location.
96331.m: With anycast, a request ends up at the nearest server.

96332.q: What is it called when requested content is already stored on the CDN server?
96332.e: With a cache hit, the edge server delivers the file immediately. With a cache miss, it first has to fetch it from the original server.
96332.m: A cache hit saves the trip to the origin server.

96333.q: What is the server called from which a CDN obtains the original content of a website?
96333.e: The origin server holds the definitive version of all content. The CDN fetches files from there and distributes copies to its edge servers.
96333.m: The CDN gets its content from the origin server.

96334.q: Against which kind of attack do large CDNs often give websites extra protection?
a: Against password theft by shoulder surfing
96334.e: A large CDN spreads the load over a great many servers with high bandwidth. A flood of requests can thus be absorbed before it reaches the origin server.
96334.m: A CDN can spread overload attacks across many servers.

96335.q: Which CDN provider caused a worldwide outage of many large websites through a software bug in June 2021?
96335.e: On 8 June 2021, a customer setting triggered a bug at Fastly. For about an hour, news sites, online shops and government sites could not be reached.
96335.m: The Fastly outage in 2021 showed how dependent the web is on CDNs.

96336.q: What is the highest possible port number for TCP and UDP?
96336.e: Port numbers are 16 bits long. This allows values from 0 to 2 to the power of 16 minus 1, that is 65535.

96337.q: Which range of port numbers is set aside for the so-called “well-known ports”?
96337.e: IANA assigns ports 0 to 1023 to common services such as web or email. On many systems you need administrator rights to use them.
96337.m: The well-known standard ports lie between 0 and 1023.

96338.q: Which standard port does unencrypted HTTP use?
96338.e: By default, web servers listen for HTTP on port 80. If you do not give a port in the browser, this one is used automatically.

96339.q: Which standard port does SSH use for secure remote access?
96339.e: SSH (Secure Shell) listens on port 22 by default. Port 23 belongs to its unencrypted predecessor Telnet.
96339.m: SSH runs over port 22 by default.

96340.q: Which standard port does SMTP use to transfer emails between mail servers?
96340.e: Mail servers deliver messages to each other via SMTP on port 25. For submission by email programs, ports 587 or 465 are mostly used today.
96340.m: Mail servers exchange emails over port 25.

96341.q: What do you call the combination of IP address and port number that describes one end point of a connection?
96341.e: A socket is, for example, 192.0.2.10:443. A TCP connection is uniquely defined by two such end points.
96341.m: A socket consists of an IP address and a port.

96342.q: What is the well-known open-source tool called that you use to scan computers for open ports?
96342.e: Nmap sends targeted packets to many ports and analyses the replies. But you must not scan other people's systems with it without permission.
96342.m: You find open ports with Nmap.

96343.q: Which source port does a browser usually use when setting up a connection to a web server?
a: The same port as the server
96343.e: The client gets a free, short-lived port from the upper range from the operating system. This lets it tell many connections apart at the same time.
96343.m: Clients usually connect from a random high port.

96344.q: What is the router setting called that passes requests on a particular port to a device in the home network?
96344.e: With port forwarding, a game server at home, for example, becomes reachable from outside. But every open forwarding is also a possible way in for attackers.
96344.m: Port forwarding makes a device in the home network reachable from outside.

96345.q: In the client-server model, who normally starts the communication?
96345.e: The server waits passively for requests. The client makes a request and the server answers it.
96345.m: In the client-server model, the client asks and the server answers.

96346.q: What do you call a device with little computing power of its own that has almost all programs run on a server?
96346.e: A thin client mainly displays picture and sound and passes on input. The actual work is done by a central server.
96346.m: A thin client lets the server do the work.

96347.q: What do you call a single component whose failure brings the whole system to a halt?
96347.e: If all clients depend on a single server, everything stops when it fails. That is why important services are run with redundancy.
96347.m: A single point of failure should be avoided.

96348.q: Which device spreads incoming requests evenly across several servers of the same kind?
96348.e: The load balancer receives requests and passes them on to the server that is least busy at the moment. If a server fails, the others take over.
96348.m: A load balancer spreads the work across several servers.

96349.q: What is the common division of an application into presentation, application logic and data storage called?
96349.e: In a three-tier architecture, the user interface, logic and database run separately, often on different computers. Each tier can be adapted on its own.
96349.m: The three-tier architecture separates interface, logic and data.

96350.q: What basic pattern does communication in the client-server model usually follow?
a: A continuous data stream without a request
96350.e: The client sends a request, for example for a web page, and the server sends back a response. This request-response pattern also shapes HTTP.
96350.m: Client and server usually communicate by request and response.

96351.q: Which protocol does an email program use to fetch messages while leaving them on the server?
96351.e: With IMAP, messages stay on the server and look the same on all devices. POP3 traditionally downloads them and often deletes them on the server.
96351.m: IMAP keeps emails on the server, ready for all devices.

96352.q: In the strict sense, what does the term “server” mean in the client-server model?
a: A program that provides services for others
96352.e: In the model, a server is first of all a piece of software that waits for requests. In everyday language, the computer it runs on is also called a server.
96352.m: A server is above all a program that offers services.

96353.q: What is it called when you gain more performance by adding servers instead of using a more powerful server?
96353.e: With horizontal scaling, more machines are added that share the work. Vertical scaling, on the other hand, means more processor power or memory for a single computer.
96353.m: Scaling horizontally means adding more servers.

96354.q: Unlike the client-server model, what is typical of a peer-to-peer network?
a: Each participant is both client and server
All data is on a central computer
96354.e: In a peer-to-peer network, all computers have equal rights. Each can offer data and fetch data from others at the same time.
96354.m: In a peer-to-peer network, all participants are equal.

96355.q: Which music-sharing service, launched in 1999, made peer-to-peer famous around the world?
96355.e: On Napster, users swapped MP3 files directly with each other, and a central index helped with searching. Because of copyright lawsuits, the service had to close in 2001.
96355.m: Napster made file sharing between users famous.

96356.q: In BitTorrent, what is the server called that introduces the participants of a swarm to each other?
96356.e: The tracker stores which peers currently have parts of a particular file. The file itself does not go through it but directly between the peers.
96356.m: In BitTorrent, a tracker puts peers in touch.

96357.q: In BitTorrent, what do you call a participant who has the complete file and only uploads?
96357.e: A seeder has all parts of the file and passes them on. Someone who is still downloading is often called a leecher.
96357.m: A seeder provides a complete file for others.

96358.q: With which data structure do peers in many modern P2P networks find each other without a central server?
a: Binary search tree on a server
96358.e: In a distributed hash table (DHT), each peer is responsible for part of the keys. This makes it possible to find out who has which data without a central point.
96358.m: A distributed hash table replaces the central index.

96359.q: Which cryptocurrency, launched in 2009, is based on a peer-to-peer network without a central bank?
96359.e: In the Bitcoin network, many nodes store the blockchain together and check transactions. Ethereum only followed in 2015.
96359.m: Bitcoin works as a peer-to-peer network without a central authority.

96360.q: Which internet telephony service, launched in 2003, used a peer-to-peer architecture at first?
96360.e: Skype originally routed calls directly between the participants and via so-called supernodes. Later Microsoft switched to central servers, and Skype was shut down in 2025.
96360.m: Skype originally made calls over a peer-to-peer network.

96361.q: Why can a peer-to-peer network often scale well with many users?
a: Because every new participant also contributes resources
Because only one server is under load
96361.e: Each peer does not just download but also provides bandwidth and storage. So the total capacity grows as the number of users grows.
96361.m: In a peer-to-peer network, new participants also bring new capacity.

96362.q: On which day does spring usually begin according to the calendar?
96362.e: According to the calendar, spring usually begins on 20 or 21 March. From then on, the midday sun is a little higher each day.

96363.q: Roughly how long are day and night at the start of spring?
96363.e: At the start of spring, day and night last almost exactly the same time, about 12 hours each. This day is also called the equinox.
96363.m: At the start of spring, day and night are about the same length.

96364.q: What happens to the days in spring?
96364.e: In spring the sun rises a little earlier and sets a little later each day. So the days get longer and plants get more light.
96364.m: In spring the days get longer.

96365.q: On which day does spring begin for weather experts?
96365.e: Weather experts count in whole months. For them, spring lasts from 1 March to the end of May.
96365.m: For weather experts, spring begins on 1 March.

96366.q: Which Zurich festival drives away winter by burning the “Böögg”?
96366.e: At Sechseläuten in Zurich, a snowman made of cotton wool, the Böögg, is burnt. It stands for the winter, which should leave.
96366.m: At Sechseläuten in Zurich the Böögg is burnt.

96367.q: Which bird comes back from Africa in spring and is seen as a sign of spring?
96367.e: Swallows spend the winter in Africa. When they come back in spring, there are lots of insects for them again.
96367.m: The swallow is a sign of spring.

96368.q: Why do plants start growing again in spring?
96368.e: Plants need warmth and light to grow. In spring the sun shines for longer and the ground thaws.
96368.m: Warmth and light wake up the plants in spring.

96369.q: What rises up inside tree trunks in spring?
96369.e: In spring the roots take up water again. This sap rises with nutrients right up to the buds.
96369.m: In spring the sap rises in the trees.

96370.q: What do a tree's new leaves grow out of in spring?
96370.e: The leaves are already hidden, tiny, in the buds. In spring the buds open and the leaves grow out.
96370.m: New leaves grow out of buds.

96371.q: What colour are very young leaves in spring usually?
96371.e: Young leaves are delicate and still have little chlorophyll. That is why they shine light green in spring.

96373.q: Which of these trees is one of the first to get its leaves in spring?
96373.e: In Switzerland the horse chestnut often comes into leaf as early as April. Oak, ash and walnut take their time.
96373.m: The horse chestnut comes into leaf early.

96374.q: Which conifer gets completely new, light green needles every spring?
96374.e: The larch is a conifer that grows new needles every year. In spring they are soft and light green.
96374.m: The larch gets new needles every spring.

96375.q: What makes the buds open in spring?
96375.e: When it has been warm enough for a while, the buds start to swell. Then they open and the leaves come out.

96376.q: How do the young leaves lie inside the bud?
96376.e: There is not much room in the bud. That is why the leaves are tightly folded or rolled, and unfold as they come out.
96376.m: Inside the bud, the leaves are tightly folded.

96378.q: Which low spring flower often forms purple and white carpets in meadows?
96378.e: The crocus flowers in March with purple, white or yellow flowers. It has only a very short stalk.
96378.m: The crocus flowers early in the year in the meadows.

96379.q: Where do many early spring flowers store their food?
a: In the seeds on the stalk
96379.e: Early spring flowers have food stored under the ground. This lets them grow quickly even when it is still cool.
96379.m: Early spring flowers have food stores in bulbs or tubers.

96380.q: Why do wood anemones in the forest flower so early?
a: The trees have no leaves yet
The forest is hotter in spring
There are no bees in summer
96380.e: In spring, lots of light falls on the forest floor because the trees are still bare. Later it is too shady there.
96380.m: Early flowers in the forest use the light before the leaves come.

96381.q: Which yellow spring flower has a flower like a trumpet?
96381.e: The daffodil is a narcissus. In the middle of its flower there is a long tube like a trumpet.
96381.m: The daffodil has a flower like a trumpet.

96382.q: Which spring flower is famous in the Netherlands and planted there in huge fields?
96382.e: The tulip originally comes from Asia. In the Netherlands, huge colourful tulip fields bloom in spring.
96382.m: The tulip is famous in the Netherlands.

96384.e: The cowslip has yellow flowers in spring. Several flowers hang from one stalk like a bunch of keys.

96385.q: The squill is a small blue flower with star-shaped flowers. When does it flower?
96385.e: The squill, also called Scilla, flowers in March and April. It is one of the early spring flowers.

96387.q: Which fruit tree usually flowers before the apple tree in spring?
96387.e: Here, cherry trees often flower as early as April. The apple trees follow a little later.
96387.m: The cherry tree flowers before the apple tree.

96388.q: What falls from the fruit trees like snow after they have flowered?
96388.e: When flowering is over, the petals fall off. They then lie under the tree like snow.
96388.m: After flowering, the petals fall off.

96389.q: In which country do people celebrate the cherry blossom with big festivals under the trees?
96389.e: In Japan, lots of people sit under the flowering cherry trees in spring. This festival is called Hanami.

96390.q: Which shrub flowers as early as February and lets yellow catkins dangle in the wind?
96390.e: The hazel flowers very early in the year, even before its leaves. Its long yellow catkins release lots of pollen.
96390.m: The hazel flowers as early as February.

96391.q: Which tree do the soft, silvery “palm catkins” come from?
96391.e: The goat willow forms soft, silvery catkins in March. They are an important first food for bees.
96391.m: Palm catkins grow on the willow.

96392.q: What can a late frost do while the trees are in flower?
96392.e: Frozen blossoms can no longer form fruit. That is why there is less fruit after a frost during flowering.
96392.m: Frost can freeze the blossoms on trees.

96393.q: What does the wind carry from birch flowers to other birches?
96393.e: Birches are pollinated by the wind. The fine dust from the flowers is called pollen, and some people get hay fever from it.
96393.m: The wind carries birch pollen further.

96394.q: Which tree flowers in early summer, smells sweet and attracts lots of bees?
96394.e: The lime tree flowers in June and July. Its flowers smell strongly, and they are also used to make lime blossom tea.
96394.m: The lime tree flowers in summer and smells sweet.

96395.q: Which big yellow flower turns towards the sun when it is a young plant?
96395.e: Young sunflowers follow the sun from east to west during the day. Once fully grown, their flowers usually face east.
96395.m: The young sunflower follows the sun.

96396.q: Which red flower often grows in summer at the edge of cornfields?
96396.e: The common poppy has thin, bright red petals. It likes to grow at the edges of fields and on fallow land.
96396.m: The poppy flowers red by the cornfield.

96397.q: Which blue flower gets its name from the cornfield?
96397.e: In the past, the cornflower often grew among the cereal crops, in the corn. It flowers bright blue in summer.
96397.m: The cornflower is named after the cornfield.

96398.q: Which alpine flower is deep blue and has flowers like little funnels?
96398.e: The gentian grows in mountain meadows and has bright blue flowers. Its flowers are shaped like little bells or funnels.
96398.m: The gentian flowers deep blue in the mountains.

96399.q: Which summer flower has orange flowers that you can even eat?
96399.e: The nasturtium flowers orange, yellow or red all summer. Its flowers and leaves taste peppery and go into salads.

96400.q: Which shrub turns whole slopes red to pink in the Swiss Alps in summer?
96400.e: The alpine rose is a small shrub in the mountains. It flowers a strong pinkish red in June and July.
96400.m: The alpine rose flowers red in the Alps.

96401.q: Which summer plant has lilac flowers and smells so strong that people fill scented bags with it?
96401.e: Lavender flowers purple in summer. Its dried flowers keep their scent for a long time and are often put in little bags.
96401.m: Lavender smells strong and has lilac flowers.

96402.q: Which orange summer flower is used to make an ointment for the skin?
96402.e: The pot marigold flowers from June into autumn. Its flowers are used for a healing skin ointment.
96402.m: Ointment is made from pot marigolds.

96403.q: In which season are most apples harvested?
96403.e: Apples need the whole summer to ripen. Most varieties are picked in September and October.

96404.q: Which festival do many people celebrate in autumn to give thanks for the harvest?
96404.e: At harvest festival, fruit and vegetables are often brought to church. People give thanks for everything that has grown.
96404.m: At harvest festival people give thanks for the harvest.

96406.q: When is cereal such as wheat usually harvested in Switzerland?
96406.e: Wheat is ripe in July and August. Then the ears are golden yellow and dry.
96406.m: Cereal crops are harvested in summer.

96407.q: Which big machine harvests cereal crops in the field?
96407.e: The combine harvester cuts the crop and at the same time separates the grains from the straw. It combines both jobs, which is where its name comes from.
96407.m: The combine harvester harvests the cereal.

96408.q: Which big, often orange vegetable is harvested in autumn and hollowed out at Halloween?
96408.e: Pumpkins grow all through the summer. In autumn they are ripe and are harvested.
96408.m: The pumpkin is harvested in autumn.

96409.q: What do farmers cut in the meadow in summer and dry as food for the winter?
96409.e: Dried grass is called hay. Farmers feed it to their cows in winter, when nothing grows outside.
96409.m: Hay is dried grass for the winter.

96411.q: Which fruits are gathered in Ticino in autumn and sold as hot “marroni”?
96411.e: The sweet chestnut grows mainly on the southern side of the Alps. Its roasted fruits are called marroni.

96412.q: Which tree is on the flag of Canada and famous for its red autumn leaves?
96412.e: The flag of Canada has a red maple leaf on it. In Canada, whole maple forests glow red in autumn.
96412.m: The red maple leaf is on the flag of Canada.

96413.q: What colour do birch leaves turn in autumn?
96413.e: The birch turns bright golden yellow in autumn. Its white bark and yellow leaves are easy to recognise.
96413.m: The birch turns yellow in autumn.
